div.head: Part 1
I.—ON GOING OUT OF TOWN.
div.stage: The Scene represents the Parlour, Hall, and doorsteps of a genteel house in the suburbs of the Metropolis. Various boxes, done up in white and corded, also portmanteaus and carpet bags, also a bonnet-box, and a bundle of umbrellas, sticks, and a fishing-rod, are disposed in the Hall.

sp.speaker: Mr. Naggleton
sp.p: Now, Maria, it is 9 o'clock.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.stage: (looking as objectionable as a woman always does when she has a travelling dress on, no gloves, and a cross aspect.)
sp.p: Well, what if it is?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Train starts at 9:40.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That's ten minutes to ten.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, it isn't.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Yes, it is.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I tell you it is twenty minutes to ten, and we have got to get to the Station.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You need not tell me that. Do you think I suppose that the train starts from this door?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No; but if we are to catch it, we ought to be off.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What nonsense! As if we should be three-quarters of an hour going there.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Why no, for if we are, we shall miss the train by five minutes.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No, we shan't, but you are always in such a fidget, and you like to be an hour before time.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Better so than an hour after it. Are you ready?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I don't know. What's that noise?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: The Cab. I sent for it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That you might have to pay the man for waiting half an hour. Just like you.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: If you are going to keep him half an hour, say so.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What then?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Then, I'll go into the City, and we will adjourn our departure till to-morrow.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If I don't go to-day, I won't go at all.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: If you don't go to-day, it will be your own fault.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No, it will not; it will be yours.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: How the—I mean how do you make that out?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Why, you keep nagging at me, and bewildering me till I don't know whether I'm on my head or my heels. Have you got the bunch of keys?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I've never seen the bunch of keys.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I gave 'em to you in the bedroom.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You did nothing of the kind. There they are in your basket.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Then you must have put 'em there.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: How could that be when you had the basket on your arm all the time. But you've got them—what else have you got to dawdle for?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Oh, there! I declare I had rather stay in town all the rest of my life than be hunted and driven like this. Have you written the directions for the luggage?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Lor, woman, yes, and stuck 'em on an hour ago.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I dare say they'll all come off in the journey.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I dare say they'll do nothing of the kind.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You know they all did when we went to Boulogne.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I know that one did which was your own putting on. Mine I pasted firmly on that occasion, and they are on the boxes now.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Yes, disfiguring them, and making them look like I don't know what.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Can't we finish the Boulogne dispute in the cab, as the time is getting on? But you like to be late—you think it fine.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: How can you talk such rubbish?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I ask you again what the—what are we waiting for?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: We are waiting till I am ready, and are likely to wait till then.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I wish I knew within half an hour or so how soon that would be, because I would like a stroll and a cigar.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You would vex the soul out of a saint.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I never had the chance of trying. But, my dear, I should like to go to Worthing to-day, unless you have any strong objection.

div.stage: (Rings.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What are you ringing for?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Sarah, to see the boxes in the cab.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: She is up-stairs with the children.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: What business has she there?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I sent her.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Pray, what for? Where's Carter, whose business it is to attend to them?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Perhaps, Henry, you will permit me to manage my servants in my own way?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It seems to me that they manage you.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I can't answer such vulgarity.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I know you can't answer what I say. But, once more, who is to attend to the boxes, if you send the servants out of the way in this ridiculous manner?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You have no more feeling for your children than a stone. I desired the servants to stay up-stairs with the poor things, that they might not know that we were going away.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Pack of nonsense, they must know it half-an-hour later, and what's the sense of spoiling children in that absurd way?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It's very little chance our children have of being spoiled, Henry. I do not suppose that there is another father in this terrace who would be happy in leaving town without taking his children with him.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Now, how in the name of everything that is—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Your language is getting perfectly horrible, Henry. They say such things are a sign of incipient softening of the brain. I hope it may not be true, but Dr. Winslow is certainly an authority.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Bosh! I was only saying how could the children have gone with us, when James expressly said in his invitation that he had only one room to offer?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And you were so eager to accept that invitation, while if we had accepted Aunt Flaggerty's, we could all have gone; but Aunt Flaggerty doesn't fish, and smoke, and drink gin-and-water in the evening.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It may be so.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry! If you dare to insult a relative, who is so dear to me, in your own mind, common decency might induce you to keep such sentiments to yourself.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I never said a word against the old lady. But I certainly had no great inclination for evenings of reading Alison, and soda-water and bed-room candles at half-past nine.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Of course you think of nobody but yourself.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, I think of you, and how pleased and amiable you will look when we get to the terminus and find the doors closed, as we certainly shall.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: We shall do nothing of the kind.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I believe you are right, we shall find them open again, and the clerks giving tickets for the next train, which does not go to Worthing.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It will be all your own fault if we do, standing here annoying me instead of putting the boxes into the cab.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It's not my business. Let the servants do it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: There, hold your tongue. I will do it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Maria, are you mad?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It is enough to make me so, being nagged and worried as I am.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Here
, Cabman!

sp.speaker: Cabman.
sp.p: Here you are, Sir!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I know that, but I want you here. Put these things in and about the cab.

sp.speaker: Cabman.
sp.p: Heavy load, rather, Sir, ain't it, Sir? How many might be going, Sir?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: There might be twenty, but there are but two.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That is right, Henry, and just like you. Standing to exchange wretched jokes with the lower orders, and every minute valuable, if we are to catch the train.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Go ahead, my good fellow. I'll make it right.

sp.speaker: Cabman.
sp.p: All serene, Sir.

div.stage: [Attacks the boxes.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That's just like you, Henry. First you joke with an inferior, and then, of course, you undertake to pay him whatever he may try to extort. Yesterday, poor Peter could not have a new cart, because it was throwing away money, but his father can give anything to an insolent cabman.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: We shall have a break-down with all that luggage as sure as eggs is eggs. Ah, the first Mrs. Naggleton travelled with one portmanteau.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: The second Mrs. Naggleton happens to be a lady.

div.stage: [At this point the conversation of course begins to grow too terrible for publication, but they get off at last.

div.head: Part 2
II.—AT THE SEA-SIDE.
div.stage: The Scene represents the Breakfast-Table at Mr. and Mrs. Naggleton's lodgings at a Watering-Place. The distinguished couple at breakfast.

sp.speaker: Mr. Naggleton
sp.stage: (who is justifiably cross, because he went out late to buy a “Times” and all the copies had been sold to unknown persons, whom he therefore hates).
sp.p: What bad tea!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: There's coffee.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: That's worse.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It was not my fault that the water didn't boil, I suppose.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No. But I suppose it was your fault for using water that didn't boil.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Do you want to have a fire in the parlour with the thermometer at 70°? or do you wish your wife to go down into the kitchen of a lodging-house, and heat the kettle?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I only wish to have decent tea or coffee.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You have managed to drink both, such as they are; so if I were you I would say no more about it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I am much obliged for your advice, and should be more obliged if you would condescend to attend to what I believe is a woman's department.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If you had gone to an hotel, you could have had all the luxuries, the want of which makes you so amiable.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I didn't choose to go to an hotel.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Then you must take things as you find them.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I have had good breakfasts at the sea-side in other days.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am happy to hear it. That makes it all the fairer that you should sometimes put up with bad ones. Not that the breakfast has been bad to-day, only your temper.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I say it has been bad. The shrimps were anything but fresh.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Do you wish me to get up early in the morning, and go out shrimping?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I certainly wish you would get up early in the morning, as it is ridiculous to be breakfasting at ten o'clock at the sea-side.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I don't see why people should come to the sea to make themselves uncomfortable.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Nor I; nor why they should make other people so.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Well, as you are in a sweet humour, I shall take my novel and go down to the beach and read, and perhaps you'll be in a happier frame of mind by lunch-time.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: When a novel-fit is on you, it is useless for me to expect any attention. If you imitated some of the perfection you are so fond of reading about, it might not be amiss.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Very neat, dear, and very new, and very much calculated to make an impression.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (who is, somehow, getting the worst of it, and is aware of the fact.)
sp.p: Of course. Any scribbler's sentiments have more weight with you than your husband's.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Well, dear, I am not unreasonable. I do not ask you for sentiments. Sentiment at your time of life would be about as suitable to you as leap-frog.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Pray don't let that anchovy paste come up any more—it is not fit to be upon the table.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You bought it yourself.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Because I could get nothing else provided for me. I shall throw it out of window if I see it again.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Pray do, or commit any other act of boyish impatience. I suppose you conduct yourself in that ridiculous way in the hope of seeming younger than you are.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, my dear. I have given sufficient proof, in the later part of my life, of not being as wise as I ought to be, considering.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Have you, love? Never mind. It's too late for regrets now. But
sp.stage: (arrested in the midst of her victory, and angrily)
sp.p: it's too early to begin smoking that abominable pipe.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I observe, my dear, that the names of things vary with the temper of the speakers. This is a pipe, when you are in a rage, but it is a Meerschaum, when you are going to fill and light it, preparatory to some little domestic manœuvre.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: A man who deserved to be called a husband would not make domestic manœuvres necessary, and a husband who deserved to be called a man would not reproach a wife with any little display of kindness. However, such a thing will not occur again.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: In that case I shall lose on my fusees, and gain on my banker's book. Ha! ha!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You are easily pleased.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Then you must reproach yourself with not oftener trying what is so easy. Come, I was only joking.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am glad you mention it. I did not see the joke. Such things are not much in your way.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: A course of novels makes us critical as well as polite.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Oh, there! I didn't say it. I'm sorry I spoke. I know that you are the wit of the “Flips” Club, only don't bring your wit to me, because I am unfortunately too stupid to be a good judge of that article.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Or of any other—potted beef included. This is the worst I ever ate.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Here is the paper, dear.
Perhaps somebody else's ideas may be more amusing than your own. Just let me see who is married.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Inhuman satisfaction!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.stage: (scorning to notice such used-up rubbish, and reading.)
sp.p: Ah! Helen Sanderson's wedding at last! Alfred has got his step, then. What a happy wife she will be.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, and will deserve her happiness. I do not know anyone with such a sweet temper. She is always cheerful; always tries to make the pleasantest answer that can be made, and looks happiest when she has done anyone a kind turn.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And she marries a man who can appreciate those qualities, and who is worth pleasing. And how handsome Alfred Crowhurst is. He looks like a gentleman.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, it is a very good imitation.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: There now, that is just like you. So spiteful. As if anybody complained of you for being only five feet four, and being obliged to wear a wig. Do allow good looks to other persons.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I have told you repeatedly, Mrs. Naggleton, that I am five feet six—not, of course—ha, ha—that it signifies; but it argues a determination to be disrespectful when a person continues to repeat what is not truth.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Well, you shall be six feet if you like, dear. As you say, what does it signify? And your wig's your own hair; and is there any other truth that you would like me to admit, while I am about it?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: If you have done with the paper, I shall be obliged by it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: There it is. I see old Mr. Bloker is gone at last. She will be well off, won't she?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: What, John Bloker! Dear me, I am shocked.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Well, I don't know what about. It must be a happy release for himself and his friends. Mrs. Bloker will marry again, I dare say.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Why, she's as old as you are. Marry again, indeed! However, as there's no saying what folly a woman may commit, I make no doubt that John Bloker has taken care to fortify her weak resolution by some anti-matrimonial suggestions in his will. Goose as she may be, she is hardly goose enough to suppose that anybody would think of her except in connection with his savings. What do you think?
sp.stage: (The above charming speech delivered slowly, and as matter long since pondered.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Perhaps you are right, Henry. Indeed, I have no doubt that you are. I spoke hastily when I said—my dear Henry! Your Meerschaum is nearly out. I'll get you a match. But won't you come and smoke on the beach?—I don't mean about the smell in the curtains, dear, because I rather like that,—it seems so domestic—but it is so much pleasanter to have you with me, and you can read your Times just as well in the shade of the bathing machines. Come, I won't be a minute putting on my hat, and as we go down, we'll call at Pickleton and Larder's for a moment, as I told them to get something which I think you'll like for breakfast— you don't half take care of yourself, and I believe I am wrong in leaving you to yourself so much, only you are so decided and imperious, dear, that I am always afraid to interfere. There—now you have a capital fire, and I won't be a minute.

div.stage: (Exit.)

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I believe that she cares about me a great deal, and that the thought of Mrs. Bloker's bereavement touched her feelings. She's not a bad sort of woman, though nothing like Mrs. Naggleton No 1.

div.stage: [Exit to wait at street door.
Scene in another apartment. Mrs. Naggleton before the looking-glass.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If he has! and he is quite capable of it. As old as I am indeed! Well, it's no use talking, but—

div.head: Part 3
III.—ON THEIR TOUR.
div.stage: The Scene represents the Interior of a First-Class Carriage. The distinguished Couple have it all to themselves, and are going from one Seaside place to another at an hour's distance.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Naggleton.
sp.p: Of course you've left the keys behind.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Why of course? Because you always do? It happens that I haven't, for here they are. What else may be left behind I can't say.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No, you took care to have business to go out about when you might have helped me in packing.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, for the last time I made the offer, you sent me packing myself. Ha! ha!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You intend that for some kind of joke. I suppose. It would be a very good thing if people didn't attempt what they don't understand. But because Wyndham Wareham says clever things, all the “Flips” club must try to imitate him, which is very pitiable.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I thought, my dear, that having
so many accomplishments, you could afford not to set up for a judge of wit.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I know real wit when I hear it, and I know that it is very unlike the ridiculous and vulgar banter that passes for it at the “Flips,” at least if I may judge by the specimens you bring home, though to be sure you may spoil them in bringing; likely enough, considering the state in which you come home.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: There are so many counts to that indictment, my dear, that I will plead to the last only, and say that you never saw me the worse for what I had taken at the little social meeting that always excites your spite.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I didn't say you were the worse. On the contrary, if you come home rather foolish, you are good-natured, and not much inclined to talk.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Your amiability, my dear, is an encouragement to me to persevere in pressing these little holidays upon you. A cheerful companion more than repays any trouble or expense she may occasion.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I understand your manly and generous meaning, Mr. Naggleton. But I am neither vexed nor surprised. I require no new proof that your earlier life was not passed in good society. The idea that, in return for her railway fare, a lady is to amuse you, is so essentially commercial that it would make one smile, but that the children are in daily danger of imbibing such lessons.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: If they imbibe nothing worse than my teaching, Mrs. Naggleton, they will do no harm. I can't say as much if they imbibe what I have seen you giving them at lunch, namely, Burton ale.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I believe that I am responsible to their medical attendant for their dietary, Mr. Naggleton.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Has your own dietary included a dictionary, swallowed by mistake, my love? Because you are bringing out the long words, uncommon, this morning.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I can well understand
that you had no such complaint to make of the first Mrs. Naggleton. I think she spelt coffee with the same letters as cough, did she not, dear?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It's untrue. And whatever she spelt coffee with, M'm, she made it with hot water, which is a precious deal more than I can get her successor to do.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Her successor should have been a kitchen-maid, my dear.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, in the matter of tongue and temper, that might have involved no great change in my present happiness, my love.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Wyndham Wareham must have given you quite a heap of his old sayings, which he has worn threadbare, and can't use any longer. Are they the perquisites of his followers? You come out quite smart in them. What a pity it is you forget them before company, and try nonsense of your own!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Ah, my dear, when we want to wound we shouldn't show that we are in a rage. Calm yourself down to your usual ill-temper, and you may be more disagreeable. At present you are a study— and I may add, thanks to sea air, a brown study.

div.stage: [Proud of his victory, he begins to read the paper, elaborately.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If anything should happen to you, Henry, I will try to forget all the insults you have rejoiced to heap upon me. But you will make that duty very, very, very difficult.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Indeed, love? Well, I promise you this. I'll try and postpone it for you as long as I possibly can.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Yes, it is very well to talk so, but I assure you, Henry, the thought comes to me very often, and prevents my taking notice of many and many a thing which I ought to resent.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Deuce it does? You resent most things, and grumble at the rest. What was that station we passed?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Tinkleby. Couldn't you read that? How your eyes are failing, and what childish vanity not to wear spectacles.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Vanity. Ha! ha! what have I to be vain of?

div.stage: [Meaning a bitter satire on his matrimonial acquisition.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I really don't know. And pride, which is a nobler thing, I do not suppose you are capable of feeling. I have read that it is much dulled by the instincts of commerce. Certainly Wyndham Wareham, your model, did say that you had reason to be proud of your marriage, but it is not for me to recal such expressions of opinion.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, strictly speaking, my dear, it is not, but their rarity shall be your excuse. And Wareham's so good a judge on conjugal matters that he has kept himself single, and means to do so.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Ah! a joke redolent of spirits and water and tobacco-smoke, and would suit the “Flips” at two in the morning.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Your ridiculous animosity to that harmless meeting is perfectly unaccountable, Mrs. Naggleton.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Animosity?—no. But I regret that the children are liable to hear, through servants, who may learn it from tradesmen, that you are in that kind of society. I wish you could pass by another name than your own among such a set.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Set! By Jove, Mrs. Naggleton, you talk as if you had been born in the purple—that is to say, to suit your understanding, as if your uncle had been a marquis instead of a man—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: The department of the medical profession more especially pursued by my lamented uncle, is one which can afford to disregard the scoffs of vulgarity.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Another burst of dictionary talk. Do you think it proper in a first-class carriage? If you cut your words in proportion to the fares, I should like to travel third.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I make no doubt that in the third-class carriage you would find companions who would suit you. You might even fancy yourself at the “Flips,” humbly listening to Wyndham Wareham.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: That's about the tenth time you've dragged in that man's name by the head and shoulders. What has he done to offend you?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: He? Nothing. I shouldn't speak to him if we met, for I think him a bad style of man, and though one rather likes anybody who is first in his way, it is really such a very small triumph to be first at the “Flips,” that I cannot make a hero out of Wyndham Wareham. Perhaps I should, like you, if I looked at him through a glass of spirits.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I had thoughts of withdrawing from that club, Mrs. Naggleton, but I am now resolved that I will accept the invitation to take the chair at the next monthly meeting.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Lor, why shouldn't you. I dare say you will not make much of a failure. I know Edward Clarkson took it, and they say did very well, and you know he is the greatest idiot in the world.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, Madam, he is not. That name belongs to a man who did not know when he was well off, but must needs—

sp.speaker: Guard.
sp.p: Tickets, all tickets ready.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I gave them to you. Why don't you get them out?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I shall get them out when they're wanted, and not till then.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You have no right to delay the whole train by your petulance.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Haven't I? But I shall, if I please.

div.stage: [And she does please.

div.head: Part 4
IV.—AT BRIGHTON.
div.stage: The Scene represents an Apartment in a Hotel at Brighton. Mr. Naggleton has put on his Hat and Gloves, placed the “Times” under his left arm, and his cigar in his mouth, and he now takes his stick, and is about to go out. Mrs. Naggleton, who is reading the Supplement, has carefully watched all his preparations, but has abstained from speaking until he is quite ready to go.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Naggleton
sp.p: I want a cheque, Henry.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Very well, my dear, I'll give it you when I come in.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I want it now, if you please.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: O, bother, won't it do an hour hence?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: For the third time, Mr. Naggleton, your wife has to solicit money from you. If you wish her to request it upon her knees, you had better state that such is your wish.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (throwing down cigar, stick, and “Times,” and tearing off his gloves.)
sp.p: How can you use such idiotic language? Why couldn't you have mentioned it before one had one's hand on the door.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am too well aware of what would have followed any allusion to the subject during your breakfast, Mr. Naggleton. I should have been insulted for not letting a man have time to swallow his coffee before dunning him for money.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Where is that wretched ink-stand? You are always shoving it out of the way.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I will fetch it from the bed-room. I do not regard a sixpenny ink-stand as an ornament to a sitting-room. I will fetch it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Readily enough, I make no doubt, now. Yesterday, when I wanted to write a note, you had not the slightest idea where the thing could be, and referred me to the waiter who seemed on such good terms with me.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That a person calling himself a man should bottle up such trifles to reproduce them for the purposes of malice!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Never mind what I bottle, my dear; get the ink-bottle.

div.stage: [Laughs.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Oh, dear! I know not which is worst—such seriousness or such joking.

div.stage: [Exit.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (which shows wives that it is unwise to leave a man to his own reflections when money is wanted.)
sp.p: By the way, what the deuce does she want with another cheque to-day? It's only Thursday. I pay the hotel bills. I don't quite see it in that light. Any how, we'll hear.

div.stage: Re-enter Mrs. Naggleton, with the ink.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: There is the ink-stand, Henry.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I say, my dear, I move that this House do go into Committee of Supply.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Just what I want, Henry. There is paper.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, no, I've got my cheque-book.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You have. You had no packet by this morning's post, and last night you had left your book safely locked up in town. But I never profess to understand the mysteries of commercial matters. I have no doubt it is all right. Draw for twenty pounds, if you please.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: This is Thursday, Maria.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am perfectly aware of it, Henry, and I deeply regret that your keeping me company here should deprive you of the happiness of attending at the “Flips.” Had you not better go up by the 3:30 train?—you will be in time to applaud Mr. Wyndham Wareham's first joke.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: This is Thursday, Maria, and you had a cheque on Saturday. Why do you want another so soon?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Because the last is spent.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Unless you have any very special reason for wishing it, I should prefer not drawing until Saturday.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: As you please.
That it should come to this!

div.stage: [Handkerchief demonstration.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Come to nonsense, Maria. Can't a husband ask a plain question without a wife's turning on the water-works.

div.stage: Mrs. N. does not speak, but the paper quivers with her shuddering remonstrance against his unfeeling vulgarity.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Now, don't be childish, there's a good creature?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Creature, indeed!

div.stage: [Heavy sigh.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I rather suppose myself to compliment you by talking to you in a business-like way—letting you into my little confidences—but one never knows how to deal with a woman. There is the cheque, however, Maria. They'll cash it for you down-stairs.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No, no. Take it back, and let us pay our bill and return to London by the third-class train. Ring for the bill, if you please.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Now what's up?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O Henry, this is your mean way of acquainting me with your embarrassments, perhaps ruin. What is to become of the poor children? Pray, ring for the bill.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: And a strait-waistcoat to follow. What are you talking of?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If your affairs are in such a state that it signifies whether you draw for such a trumpery sum forty-eight hours sooner or later, we can have no business in a house like this. Pray let us go to London, and see what is to be done.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Mrs. Naggleton, I do not quite like to say what I think you are, but certainly you are not a blessed wise person. What on earth have I said to justify such nonsense? I usually prefer to draw on Saturday because a good deal of money is paid in to my account on Fridays,
sp.stage: (observes Mrs. N. making a mental memorandum of this statement)
sp.p: that is, on some Fridays—and so—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O, don't take pains to mystify me, Henry. I told you I knew nothing of commercial matters, not even how a book could get out of a locked drawer and come to Brighton without hands. I only spoke for the sake of the children, of whom you never think.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, of course not, except from ten to six every day of my life, when I am working my hardest for them and their mother.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am sorry we are such burdens to you.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Who the D, yes, a large D, Mrs. Naggleton, for the case deserves it—who ever said you were burdens? You have no right to charge me with want of heart.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If I seem to have done so, dear, I have expressed myself unfortunately. You have heart enough, it is your poor head that is too often in fault.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (At least twenty times more enraged with this imputation.)
sp.p: I—I—am very much obliged to you, Maria; but your opinion of my intellect is, excuse me, not so valuable as it might be, if your own were of a higher order.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Recrimination, Henry, is ever the resort of irritability, but it is no argument.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Argument, indeed! No, I do not know that I am called to argue with my own wife as to whether I am a fool or not.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No, dear, it is not necessary.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: And, although your opinion on the subject is valueless, it may be well for you to know that it is certainly not that of my friends.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I learned some lines when I was a little girl—I partly forget them—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Not marvellous, my dear, considering the time that has elapsed.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: They were something like this:—“No listening senate heeded what he spoke, But the club hailed him master of the joke.” To be sure you are not master of the joke where Mr. Wyndham Wareham is, but I daresay your friends (as you say) at the “Flips” would give you a character for a sort of smartness. I alluded, however, to real intellect; and perhaps as you do not quit understand me, we had better change the conversation. What a funny noise that man with bullseyes makes.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Maria, you of all women in the world!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: My dear Henry, I have no affectation, but you are always using the word woman. It is not quite the thing, and although it is natural that you should from your antecedents—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Hang my antecedents, Madam. Look at your own relatives.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: To see that you have studied grammar if only for the sake of buffoonery is so gratifying that I abstain from further remark.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I was going to say, Mrs. Naggleton, that you of all ladies in the world are best entitled to deem me unwise, but that you also of all (O ladies) ought to feel bound not to use your privilege.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Which means, I suppose, that having honoured me with your alliance, I am never to express my sense of some of your deficiencies.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I know of none.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Ah!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: But I know that many women envy you.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Envy is always a proof of weakness of mind, and in this instance most particularly.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I tell you one thing, Mrs. Naggleton, in the old times my holidays were periods of unmixed enjoyment, now they are occasions of incessant wrangle.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If the first Mrs. Naggleton had neither sense to perceive your deficiencies nor spirit to point them out, Henry, it is not my fault that I am successor to one who seems to have been but few removes from an idiot.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I wish there were more idiots in the world.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I daresay you will find plenty down there; at least it is about the time the nurserymaids and that sort come out! Have you spoken to your friend the waiter about dinner, love?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I think I shall go up to town.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: As I was quite sure that you would not dare to be absent on a night when Wyndham Wareham is in the chair, I arranged to take an early dinner, and go round to Sarah Baltimore's.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You might have asked me first.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I might certainly, but it did not occur to me to do so. Still, I can send Sarah a note if you find by-and-bye that you have courage to stay at Brighton with your wife, in spite of your friends and their sarcasm. Please yourself.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It being matter of perfect indifference to you?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: My feelings being matter of perfect indifference to you, I seldom trouble you with them.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Such is life? And what is marriage?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Well, if you ask me, I should say it was—wedlock. Go and take your walk, and see if you can bring in a better definition, and, anyhow, bring in some better prawns than those you bought yesterday.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Cuss prawns.

div.head: Part 5
V.—AT HOME.
div.stage: That is to say, just at home. For Mr. Naggleton, as his wife had foreseen, did run up from Brighton to the meeting of the “Flips,” and, as his wife had not foreseen, did, in an accession of midnight geniality agree to run over with Mr. Wyndham Wareham to Paris for a week. He loyally apprised Mrs. Naggleton of the fact, and promised to rejoin her at Brighton. Mrs. Naggleton instantly came to London, and, on the night of the following interview had gone to a party. The scene is in the parlour at South Kensington. Mr. Naggleton has been pacing the room for about two hours, occasionally smoking, trying to read, and looking savagely at the clock. At length wheels are heard, and Voices of the Night, and a huge ring at the bell.

sp.speaker: Male Voice
sp.p: I have rung. Mind the horse, Richard. Don't get out till the door is opened, Mrs. Naggleton.

sp.speaker: Female Voice.
sp.p: Come and see me soon, there's a dear.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Naggleton.
sp.p: O, I will. There they come.
I am so much obliged to you for setting me down.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: A pleasure I propose to myself, Madam, directly.

sp.speaker: Two Voices.
sp.p: Not at all—most happy. Good night, good night. Home, Richard.

div.stage: [Exeunt wheels.
Enter to Mr. Naggleton, Mrs. Naggleton full dressed, followed by the housemaid.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Naggleton
sp.stage: (coolly as if she had not seen the hat, sticks, travelling bag, &c., in the hall).
sp.p: O, you at home. You might have opened the door, I think, instead of giving Captain Silverdale the trouble of getting out on such a night in his dress boots. Carter, is the gas lighted in my room?

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.p: Yes, M'm, some time. I thought it would warm the room, M'm.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am glad somebody has some thoughtfulness. Take up the mantilla, and fan. I am coming up directly.

div.stage: [Exit Carter.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You will stop, if you please, Mrs. Naggleton. I have something to say to you.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Won't it keep till the morning?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It is the morning, Madam. Perhaps you will look at the clock, and say whether you think this is a time for a married woman to be out without her husband.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: My dear Henry, it is her husband's fault, as he might have been with her. But I can't stand talking at two o'clock on a cold morning; besides, I am tired.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I also, Madam, am tired. I crossed to Folkstone this morning, hurried from one train to another at London Bridge, went to Brighton, and on reaching the hotel, found that you had been gone a week, and that my four letters were lying there. There they are, Mrs. Naggleton.

div.stage: [Dashes them on table.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Any cheques in any of them?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Certainly not. I gave you twenty pounds on the day I left.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Then I needn't read them, I suppose.

div.stage: [Puts them into the fire.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (utters a word which not even the example of clerical novelists will induce us to set down. Mrs. Naggleton is about to retire.)
sp.p: Stop, Mrs. Naggleton, unless you wish that my displeasure should be—should be permanent, Madam.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I have no wish, except to go to bed, being tired out.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No doubt you are tired, Mrs. Naggleton. At your time of life balls till two in the morning are not particularly suited to your powers, but I dare say that you have strength left to inform me why you left Brighton, and caused me to run down on a wild goose chase in search of you.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Without remarking on the coarseness of your language, Henry, for I am really too fatigued to talk, I will merely say that if you had called at your place of business in the City—that is, if you have one, everything is kept a mystery from me— you would have found a note saying I was home.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I hastened down as fast as I could.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Then don't abuse me for not having supposed that you would act in that schoolboy fashion. After staying away a week, you might have stayed the additional hour it would have taken you to call in the City.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: This is my return for an endeavour to show you attention.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: My dear Henry, I take your intentions and all that for granted, and you need not have recourse to awkward demonstrations.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Why did you leave Brighton?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Because I pleased. It does not suit me to be left at an hotel by myself.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I wrote from Paris to tell you to ask Mrs. Baltimore to come and stay with you for the few days I should be absent.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Did you? I didn't have the letter, as you have discovered, and if I had I should have done nothing of the kind. Why am I to pay Mrs. Baltimore's hotel bills?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And after what you confessed at Brighton of the state of your affairs, I felt that it was not for two of us, Henry, to be spending money in travelling and at hotels. If you require that costly recreation, it is for your wife to make up for it by economy and self-denial.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: If you can spoil my holiday, either when with you or without you, Maria, you do. Had I the slightest wish to shorten your sea-visit?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I—don't— know, but you took the most direct means to do it. You must be out of your senses to think that I should be staying at the Bedford while you are living at the Louvre. That is indeed what you would, I suppose, call igniting the candle at each extremity.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: The Louvre! You might as well say that I had been at the Tuileries. We went to a quiet third class bachelor hotel behind the Opéra Comique, and dined at three francs. I saved so much upon the Brighton week that I actually bought you a ring with the surplus.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: As I detest Palais Royal jewellery, perhaps you will get rid of it in some other way. I am not quite a baby, to be insulted for a week, and then to have my mouth stopped with a piece of paste.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: What do you mean by insulted, Mrs. Naggleton?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What I say. A man who leaves his wife under a false pretence that he is going to town for the night, and then skulks off to Paris without giving her the chance of accompanying him, may not be the sort of person to understand that he insults her, but if he has any respectable friends he had better ask their opinion. I could see what Captain and Mrs. Silverdale thought about it, though they had too much good taste to say anything.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Captain Silverdale's opinion of what is due to a woman is certainly valuable, for his first wife had to sue him for maintenance.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: The mind that delights in the reproduction of forgotten scandals must be indeed low, but I suppose such information is part of the advantages of your bachelor travelling.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, and another part is my having been absent for a week from the grating influence of your incessant reproaches.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Do not say that word, Henry. The time for reproaching you has long gone by—we reproach only where we hope to impress. Sometimes in self-defence against unjust charges, I may venture on a word, but it is met with a violence which makes me shudder, and it is but seldom that I risk it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I never used a violent expression to you in all my life, but by Jove, if you can't see that it would make any fellow angry to get no answer to his letters, and be made run up and down to Brighton for nothing—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What is the fare to Brighton and back?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It isn't that, and you know it, a sovereign is nothing, but—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Stop the amount out of the next cheque you give me for my housekeeping, and please say no more about it. I will gladly sacrifice some little personal comfort for the sake of a cessation of attack.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Such a cruel and unfair speech requires no answer.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Being neither cruel nor unfair, it admits of none. How long have you been home?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Above two hours.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And what train did you go down to Brighton by?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: The three o'clock.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Ah! Then with all your hurry you managed to stay and dine at the Bedford, and I hope you enjoyed yourself. Perhaps you took Mr. Wyndham Wareham, and treated him, out of gratitude for his taking care of you at the Louvre.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I repeat, Mrs. Naggleton, that I never set my foot in the Louvre, and as for dinner, I had had nothing to eat since an exceedingly bad breakfast at Boulogne.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Pray don't apologise to me. If I ever petition against the squandering of money I am instantly silenced by a fierce reminder that it is you who earn it. I suppose that the children will be brought up, or dragged up, some way, though I suppose I ought not to mention the children to a father who comes home and never even asks after them.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: As if I had not seen them all two hours ago, while their mother was diverting herself at a ball.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You don't mean that you have been cruel enough to disturb them at this time of night. Are you wild?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: The fact was you woke them all up with your ringing bells and calling servants, while you were getting ready to go out at eleven, instead of going to bed as you ought to have done, and they were all alive and rejoiced to see me. Also, they were good enough not to reject some little things I brought them over.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Upon my word, Henry, you do not deserve to have children. I declare I never heard of anything so wantonly wicked in the whole course of my life.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Rather a strong expression, considering that you read the papers.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Don't tell me, I don't believe that there is a single father in the whole district of the Seven Dials who, to gratify his own selfishness, would rush in and wake up a set of poor little children in their first sleep.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Ha! ha! No, my dear, not their first, but waiting for what would have been their second, if their mother had been a little less noisy in her eagerness to go out and dance among the other young people.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It may be enough answer to your coarseness to say that I have not danced the whole evening.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I am glad that you—or partners—had so much sense of the fitness of things. I trust that you made a good supper.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Yes, for Mr. Snotchley knows how to give a good supper, and is neither profuse nor niggardly in the wrong place. He considers that half his guests are ladies, and arranges for their comfort, instead of thinking mainly of providing his male friends with the means of taking too much. It was a beautiful supper, and though its merits would have been lost upon you, I wished you had been there to take example from Mr. Snotchley how to attend to everybody.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Ah! dear man, and it is the more to his credit, as everybody makes a point of not attending to him when he gets on his legs.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If you mean that he is too much of a gentleman to condescend to retail jokes, and to repeat prepared buffoonery, you are right: he has mixed with the best society.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Mixed what? Punch, or only grog? I know he was something in some Swell's household.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: He was tutor to an Earl and a Viscount.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I never expected to feel so much pity for the aristocracy.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You may sneer, but ladies know how to distinguish between vulgar smartness and the highbred pleasantness of one who has moved in good circles. A lady near me said that Mr. Snotchley's manner reminded her very much of the Bishop of Oxford.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I don't know why it shouldn't, for Snotchley's father was a soap-boiler.

div.stage: Mrs. Naggleton considers for a moment, and then the effect of this climax of irreverence and vulgarity is too much for her, and she retires hastily.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, the idea of likening that platitudinous ass to a splendid fellow like Saponaceous Samuel! but women are as great fools in their likes as their dislikes.

div.stage: [Exit, to get in a rage because his slippers have been poked away somewhere.

div.head: Part 6
VI.—ON MOVING.
div.stage: The Scene represents the Distinguished Couple at Breakfast in their house at South Kensington.

sp.speaker: Mr. Naggleton
sp.p: The news from America is interesting, but chiefly in a political point of view. The Democrats, who, as I explained to you—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I do not wish to hear anything about Democrats. My Papa always said that they were low people, who wished to subvert the Altar and the Throne.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: But as there is no Throne in the United States—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Ah! that is just your vulgar habit of word-catching, which, excuse me, Henry, is quite apart from the manners of good society. I do wish you could take a little example from Mr. Snotchley.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (going to be violent, but restraining himself into viciousness.)
sp.p: I should like nothing better, for he is going to Brussels.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Ah! Mrs. Snotchley is to be envied. She enjoys life.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You can enjoy it precisely in the same way, my dear.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I, Henry. No. I am not complaining—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: That's a comfort.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: But to compare the pleasurable excitement of Mrs. Snotchley's life with my monotonous existence is perfectly absurd.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Comparisons are odious, my dear, and so is bad temper. But I merely meant to say that on the present occasion Mrs. Snotchley's pleasurable excitement will be derived from reading the letters her husband may write her from abroad.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: He writes beautiful letters, for he is a man of polished education, and it is delightful to read them. And it is very considerate of him not to drag her abroad with him in this uncertain weather.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: One man may steal a horse and another is hanged for looking over a hedge.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I have heard, that wise men make proverbs, and—those who are not wise men— quote them. I do not affect to understand your meaning.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, there is no affectation about you, everybody knows that. I mean that Snotchley is praised for leaving his wife at home, while I was abused for doing the same thing.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That is what a man calls an argument! The weather during your Paris trip was lovely.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It rained four days out of six.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: The Paris letters in the Times did not say so, Henry, but I have no wish to convict you of deceit. We have more important matters to speak of.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: More important than my character for honesty and truth, Madam! What do you mean by that?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Do not be so violent. Suppose the children heard you.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: How can they hear me, when they are in their breakfast-room?—you talk nonsense.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Wives always do, of course; do not the “Flips” hold that as an article of belief? But this wretchedly built house allows everything to be heard from one room to another, and that brings me again to what I wanted to say. Have you given notice to the landlord?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Notice of what, that we can hear through his walls?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Notice that we leave his house at Lady-day.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Certainly not, because we don't.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: That is my name, Maria. It was given me by my godfather and godmother at my baptism.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I must leave the room, of course, if you indulge in such profane language.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Is that the way to speak of your catechism, Mrs. Naggleton? I thought you knew better things.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry, be serious, if possible, not for my sake, I should not think of mentioning myself, but for that of the children for whom you profess some regard, and for whom, whether you care for them or not, the world expects you to show some consideration. It is unmanly to go off in jeers and jests when a wife is talking to you of their health and happiness.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You have said nothing about their health. As for their happiness, that shout of laughing—there it goes again—does not seem to say that they are particularly miserable.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: A child will sit up on a sick bed and laugh.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, at a doctor like Peter Grievous, and well he may. Now, are you going to quote Peter Grievous to me.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Without discussing the wit of calling a professional man like Dr. Petre Gravois by a vulgar nickname, I hope a mother may remind you of what he said.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: He said that Brompton was a relaxing air.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: He said that the air of South Kensington was relaxing.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well corrected, M'm, and thank you. We are in Brompton, but as I call the place South Kensington to oblige you, suppose you live in it to oblige me.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I hope that I know a wife's duty. It is to accept the lot which her husband may force upon her, and to live, as long as she is spared, where his caprice dictates.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Caprice! Now that is—confound it, Maria, you have no right to say that. Was it I who insisted on moving here from Bedford Square?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, I am—never mind.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry, it is well you abstained from adjuration. Let your own conscience tell you whether it was not you who insisted on moving here, and whether I did not beseech for a house lower down.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, at two hundred and ten guineas a year. To do you justice you did, but one of us was not insane.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am left utterly in the dark as to my husband's means, and it is manly in him to reproach me with having believed in his own accounts of his prosperity.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: None of that nonsense, Maria, if you please. I put up with a good deal, but not with downright falsehood and injustice. We should have been simply mad to take that house. I took this to please you. Now, where do you want to go next?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I have no wish, Henry. It matters little to me where I spend the remainder of my existence, and as I have said, it is my duty to remain with you. Let it be so, and do not give the notice. But I have also a duty as a mother, and I cannot see my children falling away under
sp.stage: (tremendous shout from the children in the next room, and clatter).

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Falling away under the table—go on. I hope Blinkitty hasn't bumped her head, though.
No, all right. Go on with your description of their misery, my dear.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It is in vain pleading to hardened levity. I will merely say that if we remain here, I shall arrange to send the boys to Leominster, to their uncle, Emmeline to my cousin at Mold, and I daresay that Mamma will receive Cecilia. You need not look so alarmed—whatever pecuniary compensation may be necessary I will retrench from my own comforts.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Blinkitty shan't go to Mold, the boys shall remain at home till they are old enough for Harrow, and as for Syllabubs, you ought to be ashamed of yourself for thinking of turning her out of the house.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It is you who turn the poor child out, and cast her on the mercies of—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Of your Mamma, eh? You did not mean that, old girl, but you've just said it. No, we'll not have Syllabubs brought up on ghosts and Calvinism.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Mamma's persuasions—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Persuasions, no, by Jove. That's not the word. I don't think she wasted much time in persuading her children, especially if their ears were within reach. Syllabubs don't go there, and that's Medo-Persic, Maria.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: We will discontinue the conversation, if you please, until I have had time to consult with my brother Cornelius.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: While you are about it, consult him about a cheque he borrowed of me on Tuesday, and was to have returned the day before yesterday. Consult your great-grandmother! Well, if you and Peter Grievous say we must go, exeunt the Naggletons. Now, then, where are we to go to?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Where you please, but in the first place, remember that our moving at all is all your own doing, not mine, and that I have offered to make every arrangement that would enable you to remain here.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I like that. And take away my children from me—what the lawyers call the rule in Shelley's case.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Really, if you will attempt what you think wit, it should be new. You tried that speech before Mr. Wyndham Wareham, and he pointed out that you had made a ridiculous blunder.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You have a pleasant memory, dear I ask you where you want to live.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I answer that it is for you to decide.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I know what that means. Well, I saw a bill up in one of the smaller houses in Russell Square. I'll look in as I go into the city.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: The truth is breaking in upon me, Henry. I will bear it as well as I can, but a woman's nature requires some allowance.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Certainly, and yours is twenty pounds a week, not a bad allowance for any woman's nature.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Yes, yes, and your incessant harping on that income confirms all my forebodings. You are going down in the world! Confess it to your wife, Henry. We women bear these things more bravely than you think, only tell me all.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: By Jove, if I were to tell you all that is on my tongue, you would hear something. What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: There! I am calm, you shall see no more tears.

Now then. We must give up this house, you say, and retire into obscurity. And although you have not said so, you wish to save the expenses of a place of business. I see your meaning, dear. Yes, Henry, perhaps that will be well, and as Russel Square is in the heart of the city, your stock-brokers and silk merchants and all that sort of people could come there after you. I would give up the lower part of the house, but perhaps you would not mind letting them ring the area bell. Never be afraid to trust a wife, Henry. You shall see how I will help you in retrenchment. I will give my canary birds to Hester Deedle this very afternoon, and the children shall be gradually brought to agree to part with Tatters. Give the notice, dear, and look at the house.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (who has been turning several colours, but none of them pleasing to the eye, and who now speaks in a low, subdued voice, being afraid to trust his tongue lest it should bolt into the field of bad language.)
sp.p: Mrs. Naggleton, there is one house which would suit you uncommonly well, and you may behold it, M'm, on the left side of the Brighton railway, near Reigate. It is called, Madam, the Asylum for Idiots.

div.stage: [He rushes out of the room, and bolts himself into what he calls his “study.” Mrs. Naggleton, with a triumphant smile, takes out “Mogg” from the sideboard drawer, and placing the map before her, measures the distances between various places and one point to which she always recurs, a Terrace near Hyde Park Gardens. We wonder whether we shall meet her there.

div.head: Part 7
VII.—ON EDUCATION.
div.stage: Scene—The Breakfast Table of combat.

sp.speaker: Mr. Naggleton
sp.stage: (reading a curious little note that he finds on his plate on coming down).
sp.p: “My dere pappa will you Bee So werry kind to take Me and hedgar to the sologcal Gardings today. do if you pleese dear pappa so no More at presnt From your afecnate Son Walter Nagleton.” Upon my honour, Maria, at nine years old a boy ought to spell better than that.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Just like you. Finding fault with the poor child's spelling instead of being pleased with his letter.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I am not pleased with his letter.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You don't deserve to be a father.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: There are several things that I don't deserve. But never mind grievances now. I consider that spelling disgraceful to a boy of nine years old.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: He is not nine.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Good gracious, he will be nine on Saturday next.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And you remember his birthday. Wonderful!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I should like to know which of his birthdays I have forgotten, or yours either, which make rather a longer list. But do you defend that spelling?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: We do not expect orthography in a child of eight years old, and I think if he shows intelligence enough to write at all, and affection enough to express himself so prettily, his father need not set himself to pick holes in the poor thing's note.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I'm a brute, of course. And you wish him to go through life putting one “f” into affectionate?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If he grows up like some people it is not a word he will often want.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Not if he writes autobiography.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That is wit, I suppose. I should think you might find some other subject for your facetiousness than your children's welfare.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It is about their welfare that I wish to speak seriously, if you would let me. Walter's education ought to be taken in hand.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I had always supposed that a boy's education was his father's business, not his mother's.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: That is too good, when you have doggedly opposed every proposal I ever made for having the boys taught anything. You and Peter Grievous together have made such a clamour whenever I suggested anything like teaching that I wonder the lad knows B from bull's foot.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I hope, poor things, that somehow they will be taught enough to preserve them from vulgarity.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, I don't stand on the bull's foot. It was a phrase of the last generation. I retract the bull, and again I say that Walter, if not Edgar, ought to go to school.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It was only the other day that you overwhelmed me with a storm of violence for hinting at such a thing, and you declared with the most shocking language that they should stay at home until they were fit for Harrow.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Maria, I insist upon your abstaining from untruth as regards me. I will not be accused of wilful and ungentlemanly violence.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: My dear Henry, I do not say that it is wilful. It was always in your nature, and is so habitual that you do not know when you are making yourself ridiculous.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes I do, sometimes.
But in the interest of the children let us speak rationally, for once. I ask you to look at that note of Walter's.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I will take care that the poor child never annoys you with another.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You should be a better judge of what annoyance is.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am a wife, Henry, not a slave, and I am in the habit of saying what I think.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: What you think will vex, you mean.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If you are vexed with good sense, it is your fault, not mine.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I am not, but with spiteful nonsense.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That you never hear from me. I do not know, of course, what sort of company you keep elsewhere. The friends whom you made by your first marriage might, I should think, have hardened you for that sort of talk.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You know nothing of them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And have no desire to know anything.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Ah! One might think Walter and Edgar were children by my first marriage, to see the way in which they are neglected.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: A mother can despise such a wicked imputation. If you could be cool for a moment, and permit me to speak, I would tell you that I have been consulting Mr. Snotchley about the children.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: And why should you consult that prig?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That prig, as you coarsely call him, has had the superintendence of the education of children of first-rate persons, and his advice must therefore be valuable.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I am not a first-rate person, and his advice may go—
— may go where it is wanted.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.stage: (looks at him, but for once makes a golden bridge for a flying enemy.)
sp.p: You cannot be so cruel, Henry, as not to desire that your children should be brought up better than you have been.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, in some senses, I do desire it. But I should not like them to be Snotchleys.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: They might be worse.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, they might be like his children, who are the most insufferable little puppets I ever wished at Jericho. Would you like to see Edgar standing on the table after dinner, reciting Paradise Lost?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Yes, if he would recite it like Augustus Snotchley.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Then I should not. I'd rather see him lie on the table on his stomach, like Walter, reading Chevy Chase in that peculiarly comfortable attitude.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Your prejudices against the man make you utterly unjust. He had no object in the advice he gave me.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I'll tell you about that when I hear what it was.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: He recommended that the boys should not be sent to school.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, he doesn't keep one, certainly.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I should be ashamed of such paltriness, Henry. He says that the schools about here are not the thing.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: What thing? The thing his notion of a school would be, silver forks, and parsing out of the Peerage?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Even if it were so, no child is the worse for knowing the names of the aristocracy.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, for when he gets into business, he'll be better able to avoid discounting their bills.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: As I believe our boys are not going into business, that radical and unjust sneer is quite beside the question.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: There are some very good schools round here. Charles Helston was saying so the other morning on the top of the bus.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And you would send a child to a school recommended on the top of an omnibus!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha! I can't be angry with you, my dear, in the face of such a noble sentiment. Yes, Helston says that there's a capital school round here in Rockton Grove—Allaby, I think, was the name, but you can send and ascertain particulars.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I need not send far. The younger children of Rhatany, the chemist, go there. I know that for a fact.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: A very good recommendation. Rhatany is a very clever man, and would certainly not send his children where they would not be well taught and treated.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Thank you, Henry. I have no wish that my children should come home smelling of rhubarb and magnesia. If I can give them nothing else, I will give them the education of gentlemen. Perhaps you would like to ask Mr. Rhatany to dinner?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I should, dev—I should like very much, only he'd be bored with such talk as is mostly heard here. Rhatany attends lectures by Faraday and Owen, and might not much care for Dundrearyism. But if Allaby won't do for you and the Duke of Snotchley, there's another good school, not much farther—the Reverend Mr. Pipus's.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: The name would be enough, but are you aware that the Reverend Mr. Pipus, as you call him, is a Dissenter?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: That's truly awful. But as Dissenters do not, for being so, as yet come under the actual operation of the criminal law, I think we might inquire whether the monster has any redeeming points.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry, I know well your levity on all serious matters, but here my duty compels me to speak. My children shall be gentlemen and Christians.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Pipus took honours at Cambridge.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: The more shame for Cambridge, Henry, to allow such things, but you know that it was always considered a low College.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Was it, dear? I didn't know. But if you say so, that settles Pipus, though he wrote a crushing answer to Essays and Reviews.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I may not approve of that work, but it is like Mr. Pipus's impertinence, living in a back street at Brompton—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: South Kensington, dear.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: To take upon himself to answer the clergy of the Establishment. I will not send the boys to be brought up as infidels and revolutionists.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I don't know that I exactly wish it. What have you to propose, then?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Any proposal of mine will of course be met with outcry and scoff.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Never mind, make one, and be a martyr.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I think that a tutor might come in and instruct Walter and Edgar for a few hours in the day.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: A private tutor. Hm. I hear the voice of Snotchley.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Certainly it was his advice. I have no one else to ask counsel from.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You're very good. Suppose I give you a little without being asked.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Pray do.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You are a very highly educated wo— no, lady—you can't deny that, for you have told me so a million times, and besides, there are your translations from Cary's Dante—no, I really beg your pardon, from Dante—elegantly written out in the green and gold album to testify to your abilities.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Pray go on. When a husband begins to praise, a wife should look out for an insult that is seldom far off.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Lord Rosse's telescope wouldn't show you one in this case, my dear. I was merely about to say that suppose you were to become the tutor, and take the boys in hand for a bit. You've handsome eyes, Maria, but you need not open them so very wide.

div.stage: [Mrs. N. is unable to speak, but rises from the table.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You've nothing else to do, you know, at least in the mornings. Teach 'em from eleven to two. It would be a delightful recreation for you.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry! Let this subject be dropped between us for ever. There are limits to the endurance of a wife.

div.stage: [Exit.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (in dastardly exultation at her slip of the tongue.)
sp.p: Yes, she is sometimes unendurable. Ha! ha!

div.stage: [Exit the brute, actually chuckling.

div.head: Part 8
VIII.—AFTER DINNER.
div.stage: A Dinner Party, given by the distinguished couple, is over, and the Naggletons have descended to the dining-room. Mr. Naggleton is lighting a cigar, and preparing to have, as he says, one quarter of an hour's comfort.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Naggleton.
sp.p: I think you might take that cigar into the library, Henry, if you are unable to go to bed without smoking. I would not be the slave to a habit, were I a man.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: There is no fire in what you are pleased to call the library.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Then I will go to bed. I suppose that a wife ought to be driven from her own dining-room.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (who has had some of the wine he has been hospitably imparting.)
sp.p: There was a time when the cigar was pronounced rather an ornament to the masculine lip, and when its flavour was declared to be rather pleasant than otherwise, “but those days have passed, Climanthe.”

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What an unmanly memory you have! Throwing into one's face any casual expression of years gone by. At any rate, I never said that a dining-room ought to smell like a public-house parlour.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I have accused you of no such vulgarity, my dear. The dinner went off tolerably well, all things considered.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: All guests considered, you had better say. But of course I never expect a civil word in return for my trouble in such matters.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I didn't know you had taken any, or my acknowledgments should have been ready. I had credited our respected neighbour, the pastry-cook, with the merit of the achievement. Accept my apologies; and as you are near the—the—if I might name it, perhaps you would push the bottle this way.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It seems to me that you have had enough of that kind of thing. I should like to see Mr. Snotchley coming back into the room after a party, and beginning to drink by himself.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: So should I, because it would show that he wasn't quite the prig I consider him. But to do him justice, he did it to my claret tonight.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I think that it was very kind of him to stay five minutes after the ladies had retired, considering the sort of conversation which Mr. Wyndham Wareham chose to set going, and which of course you must help on.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I am sure, my dear, that not a syllable was said the whole evening that a bishop might not have heard with a—a hierarchical smile.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry, you ought not to speak of bishops when you can hardly speak at all, it is perfectly wicked. And how can you say that the conversation was harmless, when Mr. Wareham was making jokes about Earls, and if he did not know that Mr. Snotchley had been tutor in an Earl's family, good taste ought to have made you restrain such talk at your own table.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Goodness me, Wareham only spoke of one idiot of an Earl. Was Snotchley tutor to the whole peerage, and answerable for all its absurdities?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Of course, you meet what I say by violence, and I have done. And now that Christmas has quite gone by, and all the return dinners have been given, I hope that you mean to stop asking people whom I don't want to see here.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Christmas being over, let us put away all Christmas feelings until next December—put 'em away in a drawer, my dear, carefully locked up with the Whole Duty of Man. Now, for the world again.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It is waste of time listening to the nonsense of a man who has taken too much wine.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I haven't. I am as comfortable as I can be under the difficult circumstances of the situation.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O, I am not going to stay and disturb you. I hope you noticed your friend, Mrs. Woodcock, looking at the table, and making private notes of the electro-plate.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Admiring your good sense, my dear.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I want no admiration from such people. I declare I turned quite hot when I saw her impertinence.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I wish those côtelettes had imitated you. They wouldn't have been bad if they hadn't been cold.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And it was so necessary for you to tell everybody that they were cold. Imagine the master of a house taking pains to point out the faults of his own table! If you had held your tongue, nobody would have known it, except those who happened to take a côtelette.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: When I tell you that one of the persons who were going to take one was Snotchley, I am sure you will be enchanted that I saved that seraphic man from an unpleasantness.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: He would have been too much of a gentleman to have shown that it was cold.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Perhaps so—he's a jolly old hypocrite —let me, to be exact, withdraw the first adjective. Your health, my dear, and congratulations on the successful banquet.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Much to be satisfied about, certainly. Giving a dinner to a heap of people one cares nothing about, and only two of whom will ever give me a sandwich in return.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Don't be cynical. Look at it through the purple light of claret, and confess that we have had a pleasant evening.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I shall confess nothing of the kind. A pleasant evening to me is either one at which I am amused, or by which something is gained.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: We'll place this in the first cat'gory.
sp.stage: (Coughs, and feels that he has really had one glass too much.)
sp.p: Yes

in the first category. We have been amused—we have laughed, I have laughed—thou—thou hast laughed, everybody has laughed. Even the acidulated drop of Snotchliness was moved to a smile at the American story of Wareham's, about the owl and the preacher.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: He was too well bred not to smile, but I could see that he was not accustomed to that kind of thing, and I am sorry that you asked him to meet Mr. Wareham.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: If I am sorry, it is for Wareham's sake, who must think him an unmitigated bore. But now, didn't your sister-in-law come out for the amusement of society?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I wish that you would not call Mrs. Charping my sister-in-law. She is no such thing, and I am not ambitious of being related to a person who tells French anecdotes across a dinner-table.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Why not, if they are good ones?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I believe that I am not an uneducated person, Henry, and I may be allowed to say that no French anecdote is entirely unobjectionable.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: She had it from a clergyman.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: She said so.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Charitable!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Charity begins at home, where I want no stories of that kind.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
