sp.p: Ah! I wouldn't impute motives, but I notice that you never care to air your excellent French accent when Julia Charping is here.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I flatter myself I know as much about French as Mrs. Charping.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Flattery is condemned by the rules of society and the ethics of the moralist.

sp.speaker: Mrs.
sp.p: Do, Henry, put in that stopper, and go to bed. You do not know what nonsense you are talking.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I do, quite well. It is the playful corcorcations, at least coruscations of the midnight Aurora, pleasing after the brilliancy of the day.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I only wish you could see yourself in such a condition. Thank goodness, the children and servants are all gone to bed.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: “And leave the world to darkness and to me.”

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O, it's no use talking to you.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Never mind that, if you are a true wife. Go on just as if it was. I assure you I am not angry with you, Maria. Angry with the wife of my bosom for telling me unwholesome truths?— perish the thought, or be it banished to the gates of Jericho and the ends of the earth.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That it should come to this!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: What should it come to, a dinner-party I mean. To a jolly kind of evening, and after all, the sweet hour of conjugal confidence and unrestrained domesticity. “When we meet with champagne and a chicken at last,” as Lady Mary has it. I say—
you are not exactly a chicken, but let us have a pint of champagne—just one pint—and so crown the festive night. Eh! There's some up, I know.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry, shall the page sit up with you.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: The Page! Buttons! The idea is amusing. I should look like Brutus and the Boy in Julius Cæsar. Does Buttons play the harp? I doubt it, unless the harp of the nation once dominoes in Palestine, at least dominant—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry!

div.stage: [Exit.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: The end of Faust, by Jove! A female voice is heard—“Henry, Henry!” I come, Grimalkin! Thou marshallest me the way that I was going.

div.stage: [Gets up to his room somehow, and we hope that nobody will ever again be angry with Mrs. Naggleton after what she has undergone to-night.

div.head: Part 9
IX.—ON A PARTY.
div.stage: The Distinguished Couple have moved, as was predicted, and Mrs. Naggleton is the mistress of a house near Hyde Park Gardens.—Breakfast.

sp.speaker: Mr. Naggleton
sp.stage: (who has been moving his chair about twenty times, and putting his newspaper before him, and to his right, and to his left, and growling unpleasantly).
sp.p: Confound this room, there's no seeing in it!
sp.stage: (Goes and pulls up the blind, frantically, to the very top, and resumes his seat with an angry look of defiance to the world in general, and the Park in particular.)
sp.p: I wished we had stayed where we were.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: My dear Henry, when elderly gentlemen find their eyes failing them, they should buy spectacles, instead of going into ridiculous rages.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Eyes failing—nonsense. Eyes don't fail in six weeks. I could see to read very well at Brompton.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You will soon get used to this room, dear. You did not like South Kensington at first. Why be so impatient? Let me give you some hot coffee.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (Well, we can't print all that his abominably suspicious look, behind the Times, meant, but he had noticed that he was receiving pleasant speeches, and had not even heard a word about the blind, so he prepared for the worst, took the hot coffee, and went on reading).

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Any news of interest, dear?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, nothing, at least nothing you would call interesting —no murders, Cresswell isn't sitting, and the reviews are not of novels, only history or some such rubbish.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Nothing about that dreadful American War?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Lor! Did you know the Americans were fighting?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Why, Henry, didn't I hear you explaining the whole story of the War very clearly to the children the other night? Do you think I do not listen to what you say?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (Wishes he were out of the house.)
sp.p: No, there is nothing important—two or three battles, and about nine hundred thousand killed in each, at least so the American papers say—but there is nothing reliable.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Is reliable a good English word, Henry? Mind, I don't say it isn't, and I really ask for information, as I know you are rather strong in grammatical matters.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, it is not a good word, but we are adopting it, and so I suppose it must be recognised.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Thank you. I must remember to use it with a protest when I am writing to Mrs. Baltimore, though she will be sure to know that I got the hint from you, and sneer accordingly.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I shouldn't trouble myself with such an amiable correspondent.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Well, of course I don't write out of any particular regard for her, but I must get out of her what day she is going to fix for her Party.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: If she asks you, I suppose she'll mention it. I believe that formality is usual, unless any new-fangled rule prevails in these aristocratic regions.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Yes, dear, but I don't want to wait for that. I want to send out my own invitations to-morrow at latest.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: This is the first I have heard of any such nonsense, and I should like it to be the last.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And so it will be, Henry. I am sure that you have had no trouble when I have asked a few friends, and I should not think it fair, when you have so much upon your mind, that you should be pestered with any trifles. Except that you may like to see the list, you shall hear nothing more about it until you come home to dress on the evening.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: The whole thing is outrageous. We scarcely have been in the house a month.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You said six weeks just now.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I don't care what I said. I say we have hardly had time to turn ourselves round in the house before you want to turn it out of windows.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What a way of talking, as if you were some two-penny lawyer's clerk in Tottenham Court Road, who has to pull down the beds, and take off the doors for supper-tables when he wants to see his friends. These houses are expressly built to give parties in, and you won't know three hours before or after that there has been anything of the kind.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: But what the deuce is the use of anything of the kind, as you call it. What do we want to give parties for?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I really can't answer such nonsense as that. If you don't mean to live as other people do, you had better have come here, but have taken a hut in Wales or some such place.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Ha! It may come to that, nolens volens, if you follow up your wise notion of doing as other people do.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You have said that kind of thing so often, Henry, that it has lost its effect with me. A man who can send twenty pounds to a Lancashire fund can perfectly well afford to do what is necessary to maintain his own position in society —or ought to be able.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Your favourite clergyman informed us, last Sunday, that a mere sacrifice of superfluity was no charity, and that we ought to give up our own pleasures for the sake of helping distress.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You had better keep away from church if you can go there for no better purpose than to distort what is said, and to pretend you are told to make charity a plea for meanness. Besides, as you say you do not consider a party any pleasure, I don't see how you can affect to be making any sacrifice.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (would like to laugh at this ingenious way of putting it, but masters himself and continues the fight.)
sp.p: Will you give me one rational reason for cramming these rooms with a heap of people we don't care about, and for wasting a lot of money on a supper? Do you want to dance?

div.stage: [Looking chronology at her.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.stage: (who decidedly means to dance, if asked, but who scorns reply to such a question.)
sp.p: If friends are to be made for the children—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Come, come. Let them alone. The children are to the mistress of a house what the cat is to a lodging-house keeper—an excuse for everything. Your eldest child is not ten, and has nothing to say to a party that begins at eleven. If you don't pledge yourself that they shall all be in bed two hours before anybody comes, I declare at once that the party shall not be given. Now!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.stage: (too genteel to think of a sprat and a salmon, but nevertheless.)
sp.p: My dear Henry, you are the master in your house, and I do not say that the children ought to be kept up, though I should, I own, just like them to be seen, but I feel you are right. They shall all go to bed.

div.stage: [Considers which morning she will be able to spare to take them to Swears's, and arrange their costume for the party.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I do wish you'd give up the notion altogether. Have a dinner-party, if you like.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Now, Henry. You spoke to the children (might I mention the children?) so nicely the other night about selfishness, and then you want to set them such an example as that! What pleasure is a dinner-party to me? I sit for two hours between two men in white cravats, who are sure to be the greatest bores of the set, and they ask me, in made voices, what I think about Giuglini, and Colenso, and Fechter, and then I go up-stairs with the ladies, and have a still stupider hour till you all come up, just in time to hear the carriages announced.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Maria, thou reasonest well. We will not give the dinner-party, either. I am eager to show you that I am not selfish.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I was thinking of Thursday, the 26th. That will be three weeks' notice, you know, only I must find out Mrs. Baltimore's night, because she knows so many of my set, and would be delighted to secure them. I suppose you couldn't see Mr. Baltimore in the City, and manage to extract it, accidentally. You are a good diplomatist, when you choose.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: If I were, this party would not take place. Praise undeserved is satire in disguise. However, name a long day, the longer the better, as that gives more chance of something happening to make it necessary to put it off.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If there is an ungracious way of doing a thing, I will say you have the knack of finding it out. Making every allowance for your early habits, it is very hard, sometimes, to be talked to as if one were a tradesperson trying to cheat you into something.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: My early habits are opposed to my sitting up till three in the morning, so don't expect me at your ridiculous party.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Then stay away.

div.stage: [Exit.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Hm.

div.stage: [Goes to business.

div.head: Part 10
X.—ON PLEASURE BENT.
div.stage: The distinguished Couple are in their Carriage (well, a hired Fly is a Carriage, ask the Tax People whether it isn't), and on their way to Covent Garden Theatre, to hear Mr. Balfe's new Opera, “The Armourer of Nantes.”

sp.speaker: Mr. Naggleton.
sp.p: Ah, old lady, we didn't get along so fast as this the last time we were here.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Are you addressing me?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Why, who else? Is there a ghost in the carriage, or any other third person singular?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I thought you might be speaking to the apple-woman by the lamp-post—you are fond of talking to the lower orders. Perhaps you will draw up the window.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I meant, as you know very well, on the Illumination Night.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If I am to have anything like a pleasant evening, do not revive the recollection of that night. I wonder that you are not ashamed to do so.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
Mrs. N.
sp.p: Very well; drop the subject.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Confound your petulance, Maria. I bear a good deal from you, because I can make allowance for your being—for your not being an over-wise woman; but, by Jove, you turn the screw too hard sometimes.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Abuse, oath, insult, vulgarity, in a breath. Say what you please to me, Henry, you know I am helpless.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I know nothing of the kind; and I don't know anybody who can help herself better. But I didn't mean to hurt your feelings. There!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It is too late in life for you to make a pretence of caring for my feelings, Henry. You never did; and the affectation is now more painful than the reality. Does Miss Pyne sing in this opera?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, splendiferously.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You have heard it, then?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Now, how should I hear it? You know where I have been every night since it came out.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I know what you have told me of your movements, but a man who is so engaged in business of importance might forget a trifle like going to the Opera.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Do I ever go to the theatre without you?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I know not. Your conscience can best answer you.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Now I'll bet a guinea that some of your mischief-making, gossiping friends have been inventing some story about me. Out with it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Your irritation is strange, supposing that there are no grounds for any accusation. And I have made none. But having attacked me, you are glad of an excuse to turn upon my friends.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: A wife's friends should be her husband's.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Not when a husband chooses—I will not say unworthy ones, but friends of a class to which she has not been accustomed.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: That's a cut at the poor “Flips.” I'm sure one of 'em did you good service on the Illumination Night, and got us out of the block, when your genteel Mr. Snotchley sat in the corner as stupid as an owl and as savage as a bear.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: The noise and violence of the lower orders were new to Mr. Snotchley, and produced a natural effect upon him, but he never forgot himself.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, that's true, he remembered nobody else, and walked into the sherry as if it was his own. But that's nothing. I only say that a “Flip” was very useful.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You mean that strange looking person in the Scotch bonnet. I was really ashamed of you, letting him lean upon the carriage-door, and giving him wine and a cigar.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Woman is incapable of gratitude, we know, but this is monstrous. Didn't he earn the sixpenn'orth of sherry by what he did with the policeman?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: He was vulgarly familiar with the man, and compromised us all.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Didn't he get the carriage moved, I ask you that?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I dare say it was just going to move without his interference.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: By Jove! We had been at that point for an hour and a quarter, and were told that the people before us had been there for two hours and a half.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I have begged you not to recal that night. Do you think that I shall ever forget that period of block, and your conduct, before the children, too?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: What do you mean by conduct? It was a long spell, and I did what I could to amuse you all.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You must have a strange opinion of me, or of Mr. Snotchley, to think that we could be amused by your exchanging vulgarities with the police-constables, or telling them that Mr. Snotchley was a wretched pugilist.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Ha! ha! I said just the reverse. I said he was Tom King, who was inclined to punch all their heads for not making way for us. Why, old Snotchley himself grinned at that, and but for you, and gentility, would have humoured the joke.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I will take care how I expose him again to such coarseness.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, as we shan't have another Prince of Wales's wedding at present, he is tolerably safe. He did not offer to share the price of the carriage, though he started the idea of our having one.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You could not have been so mean as to accept it, if he had.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I don't know that. Any how, he might have tried.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: My dear Henry, your commercial habits prevent your appreciating the subtle delicacy of a true gentleman's nature.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: May be so, and it's my misfortune that such subtle delicacy looks to me uncommonly like selfish shabbiness. However, a carriage won't ruin us.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I was told yesterday that it would.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Who by?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You mean by whom? By yourself. To be sure the carriage then spoken of was for your wife's health and pleasure, not for your own amusement.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: O, ah! Yes, when Mother Baltimore had been riling you with the sight of her glaring brougham, and working you up to believing the world would be at an end if you didn't get on wheels. That's another pair of—another pair of horses. No, my dear Maria, this particularly comfortable and easy-going vehicle does quite well for us, and is much better than taking our own carriage to theatres and so on. “We Fly by night,” as the song says.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I have heard my uncle say that stinginess and vulgarity were born twins.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: And he was an authority upon questions of birth, that excellent and lamented acc—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Accession to the aristocracy of our pedigree. But that does not alter the fact that we do not want any other carriage than that which Mr. Jobling is kind enough to have ready for us at any hour on demand, at the place inscribed Berkeley Mews, which always reads to me like a statement about a cat.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I have no patience with such puerile trash. At your age you might leave off trying to make miserable jokes. Giggling and grey hairs don't go well together.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Grey hairs yourself—what do you mean by that, Maria? I've heard one or two things of that kind from you, and I rather recommend you to discontinue the series.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: My dear Henry, you should never lose your temper, especially when you are going out for an evening's pleasure; but rather be thankful that you are still able to bear the fatigue of coming to the Opera, and that your hearing still enables you to know what is going on.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Overdone, my dear; overdone. A woman should let bad alone. When you show that you mean to wound, you break the point of the weapon.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Did you hear that weapon speech when you heard the Armourer of Nantes, dear?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Very well, Maria. As telling you the truth on all occasions is so repaid, I will be more sparing of it in future.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: My dear Henry, are you going to carry stinginess into every department. Poor me! But here we are.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Go on, can't you? The next door.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Do not be violent, dear. He knows his place. The principal door is for carriage people. The side-doors are good enough for cabs and flies.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Take care.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O, never mind if I get wet feet. We save expense, you know.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Wet feet. You were under cover.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: All right, dear. And it is very kind of you to come and be bored with a second hearing of the same opera, and I wish you had let me bring Mr. Snotchley instead, as he understands music, and you don't, but—

div.stage: [We leave them entering the crush-room.

div.head: Part 11
XI.—THE BISHOP.
div.stage: Evening. The children have just gone up to bed. Now, to reveal a secret which we cannot keep any longer, Mrs. Naggleton literally “spoke by the card” when—but you'll see.

sp.speaker: Mr. Naggleton
sp.p: Good night.
Bless 'em, they are very good children, after all.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: After all what?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: A phrase. Before all, if you like it better.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: My liking is of no consequence, but I thought that perhaps you had been nursing up some charge against the poor things.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Nonsense.

div.stage: [Begins to read Dr. Colenso.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: However, you may well say, “after all.” Considering what their father's favourite studies are, and that his conduct is of a piece with them; it is wonderful that the children's characters are not deteriorated by his example.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: What's up now, in the name of everything that's detestable?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You are polite, Henry, as well as elegant in your language.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I'm neither the one nor the other, and don't mean to be. What are you talking about?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It is a common practice with culpability to affect indignation.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Confoundedly sententious you are, Maria. If you have nothing pleasanter to say, perhaps you will let me enjoy my evening in reading.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O, you have so many ways of enjoying your evenings.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Have I? Spending 'em here doesn't seem likely to be one.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am aware that you think so, Henry. An opera-house is perhaps a more pleasant place for a father and a husband.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, that's grateful. As if you didn't make me go to the opera.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I make you! O, Henry!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Why, I swear that you gave me no peace till I got you the box; you reminded me of it at half a dozen breakfasts, and even set the child to play one of Miss Pyne's songs on the pianoforte, that you might have an additional poke at me.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What a mean mind you must have to fancy such things.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Fancy—well, when a woman says to her daughter, “I think, love, that you are playing it too fast, but as your papa will not allow me to hear the opera, I cannot be sure,” there's not much room for fancy as to what she means.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: One is never safe with you, Henry. A little playful badinage, which in good society is a lady's privilege, and which a gentleman always receives kindly and in the nicest sense, your cynical nature turns into sarcasm or hidden meaning.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Thank you, my dear, but I am not exactly a fool, and I know the difference in tone between playfulness and petulance. The tone is everything.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I congratulate you on your musical knowledge. Your frequent visits to the opera do you good.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Frequent visits? Colenso's rather hard nuts to crack, Maria, but he's easy to your riddles.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I request that you will not name that atheistic, immoral, and I believe improper book to me, however much I may be compelled to see its influence upon you.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: As you haven't read a line of it, and couldn't understand one if you had, I say nothing at your ridiculous language about one of your Bishops—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: My Bishops! Everybody knows that a Colonial bishop is nobody, a mere emigrant travelling missionary.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: One Paul was, I think, open to the same objection.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If you are going to be downright profane, you had better say so, Henry, and I will go up-stairs and sit in the cold, rather than hear you.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: But I'm not—
in spite of the temptation.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What a lady is not intended to hear, she does not hear.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I am aware of that theory of moral acoustics, my dear. I will only venture to ask you what you happen to mean—if anything, which isn't always the case—by the influence of this book upon me?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Ask your own conscience.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It is as mute as a dumb-bell on a dumb-waiter.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If a wretched joke is enough for you, we will drop the subject.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: We will not. For once, if you please, I request to know what you mean. Don't begin beating about the bush again, but tell me in two words.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I can do that, though they may be unpleasant.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Then I am sure you will. Let me hear them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Washing Tubs.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: My dear Maria. You have an aunt at Dr. Tuke's Asylum, and a grandfather who would have been looked after if he hadn't been poor, and so it's in the family, but you are breaking out in a fresh place. Are you cranky, or is this another bit of—what did you call it—spiteful badinage?

div.stage: [Mrs. N. smiles, makes no reply, but throws a small oblong yellow card towards Mr. N. It falls on the rug, but he can see printed in capital letters the words just before proclaimed by his partner.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: There are the words, certainly. Does it mean spirit-rapping?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: In a sense, yes, Henry. For it means imposture.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Washing Tubs mean imposture. Try Harper Twelvetrees's Powder.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You act well, Henry, but you have been watching much acting. You need not carry it on, however, as I know all. Had you not better take up that return check.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (the inmost recesses of his dark heart suddenly illuminated as by Mr. Way's galvanic light).
sp.p: Return check?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Yes, Henry. Now, do not attempt to delude me. I could not know there were such things, or that words, selected at random, were printed on them, and changed every night to prevent cheating by the class
who haunt the plebeian part of the theatre. But it has been explained to me, so spare equivocation.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: O!
So that's a return check, is it. Dear me. Quite a curiosity of literature. Let us frame and glaze it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I pity you. I pity you sincerely, Henry Naggleton.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (who has not decided on his line of action).
sp.p: Do you, my dear? I'm sure it's very good of you; and pity, as Shakespeare says, is akin to love.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Love! I have striven to fulfil my conjugal vow—you do not know how I have striven, Henry—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I can testify, my dear, to a good deal of strife.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: But it is a hard task to maintain love and honour where one witnesses fraud and falsehood.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Mrs. Naggleton, place a guard upon your expressions, or you may be sorry for it. I see what you have been driving at all this time. You have been, as you said of me, nursing up a charge for more than a fortnight, instead of bringing it out at once, as a loving and affectionate wife would have done, and been too glad to have an explanation.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Yes, if she could have believed it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Believe this, or don't, it's the last word I shall condescend to say. You have been searching my pockets and found that card—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Sarah found it in brushing your waistcoat.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: When?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Never mind. I don't choose to be catechised.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It is more than a week ago, for I've been wearing the waistcoat it was found in ever since Sunday.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am glad you don't deny that the card is a check. I was prepared to hear you say, with a hypocritical laugh, that it was a new kind of advertisement.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Suppose I had.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Then I should have been prepared to name the theatre it came from, and the night it was issued.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: So, Madam! You take pains to get up a case against your husband? And pray who may have been your accomplice in this domestic treachery?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Your accomplice in your own treachery, Henry. Your friend, Mr. Wyndham Wareham, your idol, and patron. You see how much your public-house friends are to be depended on.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Wareham told you I had been with him to the Gallery! Wareham told you that was the return card!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: There!
sp.stage: (Plays a second card on the first).
sp.p: There's his own, taken at the same time as yours. He gave it me. Does that satisfy you?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: He's a double-faced humbug, and I'll never go to the “Flips” again till he's expelled.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.stage: (secretly exulting at having brought down two birds with one stone).
sp.p: That is your own business, not mine. It is only my business to show that I am not to be befooled. Something told me that you had some reason for not caring about getting that box for me, but little did I think that you had left me solitary here while you had been to the theatre. I remember, as if it were yesterday, that you said, “O, do you want to go; I don't hear that opera's up to the mark”— you were handing me a piece of haddock, and your eyes were on mine as you performed that falsehood. Henry, I shall never see your eyes again without thinking of haddocks.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (recovering his temper and some of his sense, and resolved to laugh it off.)
sp.p: Haddocks— well, my dear, I admit that the thing looks a little fishy, but it can be explained in a minute, and then you'll see that there's not much to complain of.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Do I ever complain? Never, now. Those days are gone.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Don't be silly. You complain a great deal, and so you ought if you've anything really to complain of, only you haven't. See here. It was the “Flips” night, and you were not solitary, for you know I was going to be out, and Mrs. Baltimore was here. It so happened that there was nobody at the Club meeting but that inf— that inferior beast, Wareham, and myself, so we thought we'd look into the theatre, and not being dressed, of course went up-stairs. We didn't stay long, and I came home. I should have told you all about it, but you were in an atrocious temper, because Mrs. Baltimore had got leave to keep a footman.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That is right. Charge it on me.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: So I do. Somehow there was no opportunity of mentioning it in the morning, and the longer a thing is kept back the less chance one finds of telling it, so I didn't tell you. It's not often I go anywhere without you, and I suppose I have a right to go to the theatre if I like?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Such are the morals learned from atheistic books. You scoffed at Mr. Snotchley's advice to you not to read Dr. Colenso, but Mr. Snotchley knew the calibre of your mind, and that it was sure to be injured by such a work. Now you avow your conduct to have been deceitful and cowardly. I forgive you, Henry, but I should hope that you can never forgive yourself.

div.stage: [Exit.

[Mr. N. uses language which we are sure the Bishop of Natal would be the first person to reprehend, and which we have not the most remote intention of reporting. He then descends to the dining-room, to mix himself a large tumbler of brandy-and-water, and to mature a scheme for the utter discomfiture of Mr. Wyndham Wareham.

div.head: Part 12
XII.—ON THE DERBY.
div.stage: After Breakfast on the Derby Day, 1863. Rain pouring. A few Carriages are seen passing, either closed, or covered with umbrellas. Mr. Naggleton rings the bell.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Naggleton.
sp.p: What do you want now?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I want the bell answered.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Sarah is up-stairs.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I don't want Sarah.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: The cook will think it is to tell Sarah to take away.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I don't care about the cook's thoughts.

div.stage: [Rings again.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Are you not well?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Bless my heart and soul, can't I ring a bell in my own house?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You have shown that you can, I think.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, but not that I can get it answered.

div.stage: [Rings again furiously, and the Cook comes in with her eyes very wide open.

sp.speaker: Cook.
sp.p: Did you ring, M'm?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I! O dear no!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Let somebody get me a cab—a close cab—directly.

div.stage: [Exit Cook without reply.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You are very fond of preaching about consideration for servants.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I'm not fond of it, but I have to do it more often than I like.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If you practised what you preach, you would not send a girl from her work into the wet on such a morning.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You can send 'em fast enough, rain, hail, or shine, when you want to go to some ridiculous Concert. Let the boy go that cleans the boots, and does them so villainously.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If you chose to keep a proper domestic, he would do them better, I dare say.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I keep the domestics I think proper, and if you kept them in better order and check, things would be pleasanter.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Don't be angry with me, Henry, because it happens to rain on the Derby Day, and you are obliged to give up your holiday. I cannot command the weather, you know.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, nor your tongue neither, or you wouldn't aggravate a man with his head full of business.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O, I'm sure I beg your pardon. It is something so new to hear you talk about business that you must make an allowance.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (looking as if he should like to make her one, not too large, and dissolve the partnership).
sp.p: Certainly, I don't talk business to you, for an obvious reason. Why the devil don't that cab come?

div.stage: [Looks at the bell-handle.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Don't, Henry, don't. I will go for it myself.

div.stage: [Rises.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Are you out of your senses? There he goes. By Jove, she's only just got him off. That's downright insolence on the part of that woman, and you ought to send her away.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Perhaps the poor child hadn't done his breakfast.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Of course. Take anybody's part but your husband's.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am a wife, Henry, but not a slave, and when my husband is in the wrong I shall take the liberty of telling him so. Your temper is growing upon you, and unless you control it, you will become a nuisance to yourself and to all about you. If it rains, and you are disappointed of the pleasure of throwing sticks at little dolls—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Little dolls be—hanged, and great dolls, too. You know I have as much intention of going to Epsom as you have of being amiable. I can't say anything stronger.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Or weaker, dear. But you always do go, and you always say that you are not going.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I went last year, and I have been once before, since the year we were married. I tell you I want to get into the City, because I expect important letters, and I may have to see two or three men before they go off to the races. That infernal boy! I believe he is standing to watch the carriages go by.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Boys will be boys. You were a boy yourself once. And you are very like one now, in your irritation at being kept in town—don't tell me nonsense about it. All men think they are dreadfully wronged if they cannot go and make fools of themselves at Epsom.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Some people are fools ready-made, and need not go to Epsom to be manufactured.
I'll teach that boy manners!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Well, dear, one does hear strange things, but if there is one branch of education that I should have advised you to decline attempting, it is that. Calling a wife a fool over her own breakfast cups and saucers is—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I didn't. It's untrue.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And mending it by calling her something worse—but there is the poor boy in the cab —how wet he looks.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, and nicely he has wetted the cushions for me, which is a thing that don't occur to you, of course.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O, I wish it had been a fine day, and you had been able to go with your friends. It may be foolish and expensive amusement, and the company may not be fit for the father of children, but it is better than such a display of evil-temper, rudeness, and cruelty.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I'm a demon, no doubt—so don't wait dinner for me. In fact, I'd better say I'll get a chop in the City.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No, Henry, do not utter a deliberate falsehood. I will not wait dinner, that is enough.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Sweet creature—sweet temper—sweet tongue.

div.stage: [Exit, and is heard to quarrel in the hall with his Inverness cape, wrong gloves, unbrushed hat, and umbrella that won't open, and moreover to launch a passing reproach at the boy for dawdling, and to repeat his direction to the cabman angrily, because that deaf fiend has the insolence to answer, “Sir?” to the first. Then Mr. Naggleton disappears until a little past ELEVEN O'CLOCK AT NIGHT, when he re-enters the room. Mrs. Naggleton is reading Zimmerman “On Solitude,” and does not look up at his entrance.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (with some natural and some acquired cheerfulness.)
sp.p: Well, my dear, and how are you by this time?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: This time? Just midnight. O, I am very well.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Nay, only just eleven.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I presume you do not wish to sit up?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, just ten minutes, and let me have a glass of something or other, and I'll tell you a bit of fun.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am not in a state of mind for what you consider fun.

div.stage: [Rings.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Come, don't bear malice. I know I went out a little fluffy, for I had had a bad night, and something to bother me, but I didn't mean to be unkind.

div.stage: Enter Sarah.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Your master wishes you to bring him the tray, a tumbler, hot and cold water, a teaspoon and the spirits. I suppose that the kitchen fire is out. In that case you must re-light it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Never mind. Cold water will do.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Hot and cold water.

div.stage: [Exit Sarah.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: O, don't have the fire lighted.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I was abused this morning for not keeping my servants to their work. I will give no cause for a repetition of the reproach.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Reproach! Lord, Maria, how you bottle up a hasty word. Ar'n't we husband and wife? Forget and forgive—we've no time for quarrels in this world. I always do. Here's something for you.

div.stage: [Tosses nine bright sovereigns into her lap.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.stage: (taking them up, and placing them at some distance from her on the table.)
sp.p: Is that on account of the house-money?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, no, that's a hextra as the child says. That's all for yourself, to make ducks and drakes with, if you like to be orni-orni-thological.

div.stage: [Mrs. N. looks at him fixedly for a moment, and sighs deeply.
Enter Sarah, with tray, and exit.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Pray be careful with the glass jug. You had better let me mix it. Please don't spill it over the cloth. Ah! Take care of the tumbler.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: That's the way to make a fellow nervous, M'm. But no such luck. There—
—as nice as pie, and twice as wholesome. Your health. May I mix a little for you?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: For me!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Do you good. But as you like. You might say thank you for nine sufferings, though. My winnings. Mrs. Naggleton, and here's long life to Macaroni, and to Mr. Punch for prophesying that Mac would win.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I beg to decline money which, as I infer, you have won by gambling, if indeed you won it at all, and it is not a sort of hush-money added to losses of which I know nothing.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Hush-money be blowed. I won it fairly and lawfully in a sweepstake of nine, by drawing Macaroni, Mr. Naylor's horse, who, I inform you, M'm, is the Winner of the Derby, and, as I said, here's luck to him. It was a beautiful sight to see him win, and quite repaid me for a disagreeable journey. He won by only a head, and if Lord Clifden hadn't slipped, or changed legs at the last, you wouldn't have had those sovereigns.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I repeat that I decline taking gambling money. Do you wish to sit up longer?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Of course I do. I haven't done my groggums. Bet you nine to one you take the money.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Pray leave your race-course slang outside the door. It is an affectation that is perfectly ridiculous in a man who does not know one horse from another.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Maria, you're an antiphonetic—no, you are not—you are an antipathetic woman. If you had a good genial nature, you'd give me a kiss, or a box on the ear, which is all the same, and say, “I'm glad you've enjoyed yourself, my old dear, and thank you for thinking of me.” That's the way to oil the wheels of domestic life, and make 'em work pleasantly. What good whiskey this is.
You'd join chorus if you were half-jolly.

div.stage: [Slaps his knees, which is the American accompaniment to this delightful Lyric.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Pray, Henry, have some regard for our reputation, and don't let the neighbours think we keep a public house.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Ha! ha! I should like to keep a public-house, very well, and I'd hang out the sign of the Good Woman, and it should be you; for you are a good woman at bottom, in spite of your little tempers. Your health!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And so you meant to go to the Derby all the time. Of course you did. And why all that mean deceit and pretence of business, and annoyance?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Swear I didn't mean to go. But I got my work done, and some fellows came in and offered me a seat, and as—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I desire to hear no more.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, do, my dear, for it's as good as a play. In came old Snotchley, and Piggy Farmer—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry! Will you tell me, at midnight, in my own house, that Mr. Snotchley has been to the Derby with you?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Hasn't he? That's all. And came out as I never saw him before, as jolly as a sandboy, only he was a trifle wetter. There's one of his sovereigns in that heap, M'm, the lightest, I dare say, if one's lighter than the others, but he paid it and lost it, and never made a wry face.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You are deceiving me again, Henry.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Am I, by Jove? Put on your bonnet, it don't rain, and come round to his house and see. He's in no humour for bed, and we'll finish the evening there.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You must be Mad.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Not a bit. Put on your bonnet. Or, if you don't, I'll just take up this money which you scorn, and I'll go down to the Club and take nine chances for the Oaks.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.stage: (snatching at the money with a good bit of womanly eagerness and a natural laugh.)
sp.p: I'm blessed if you shall.
sp.stage: (Secures the sovereigns in a little pocket.)
sp.p: There, now, go to bed. You sha'n't make any more, I declare you sha'n't. Go up-stairs. I'll see to the things being put away. Walk straight now—the servant will see you—
—Henry! Don't!

div.stage: [What that last exclamation referred to shall never be divulged in this world; but Mr. Naggleton accepts the truce, and goes up-stairs singing, “The man that hath good whiskey.”

div.head: Part 13
XIII.—ON THE DRAWING-ROOM.
div.stage: Mr. and Mrs. Naggleton in their own Drawing-room are beheld, like Ferdinand and Miranda, playing at chess, to which, to Ferdinand's astonishment, Miranda, has gaily challenged him. Mrs. Naggleton, in emulation of Mr. Paul Morphy, is playing two games at once, but not by any means blindfold.

sp.speaker: Mr. Naggleton.
sp.p: Check to your Queen.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O, Henry! Now, that is very artful of you. How well you are playing! My belief is that you are getting practice somewhere out of the house, and that is not fair.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I have never touched a chessman since we played last. Do you mean to lose her?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No, no, dear, only give me time. I can't think as fast as you do, with your arithmetical old head. And you have fortified every point. I think, if I could spare you, that you ought to go out and help the Federals.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You have rather crowded up the Queen, my dear. She's quite holding a levée with those bishops and knights.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Now that's very funny, Henry. I call that true wit, which you can talk when you like. I must remember that, and tell it to dear Lady Pugbury.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Dear, is she? Pug was, and almost extortionate, when he kept the china-shop, and before he got knighted.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: My dear Henry, it was a wonderful porcelain manufactory, and I have heard you say that there can be no more honourable way of rising than by commerce.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes. But Pug was a humbug, and lived on other people's brains; and she's another, and I wonder you haven't found her out.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Perhaps I have, after your hints. But she is good-natured, and I am sure it was very kind of her to offer to present me.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: With what—tea cups, or soup plates?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: My dear, I come to you for all I want. I mean she has promised to present me at Court.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Present you!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Yes, me. Why not, Henry?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You be presented at Court?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Why not, I wonder? I suppose that I—
—I suppose that the wife of Henry Naggleton is a proper person to be received there, or anywhere else that he chooses to send her.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: But, my dear Maria— O, come, this is rather too ridiculous. If there were no other objection—and you can't be serious about it—you have no carriage, and the omnibus hasn't the entrée.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What a funny picture you imagine. You really ought to send it to Punch. I declare it would be capital. But there would be no difficulty and no expense, at least for the carriage, for her Ladyship would take me. I arranged that.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Your Queen is in check, Maria.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Well, dear, she won't run away while I speak to you. I want to consult you about my dress, and about jewels, because when you will condescend to give your mind to such things, you hit out a practical suggestion at once, and you do save me such a deal of trouble. What's the use of a husband, if he is not to assist one with his knowledge and decision?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: My dear Maria, you can't say that I oppose any reasonable idea of yours, but what on earth do you want to go to the Palace for?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Why, I think we owe something to ourselves.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Let us continue to owe it—ourselves are indulgent creditors.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You make me laugh, but it isn't an argument, dear. I confess I have some curiosity, and I should like to see the scene.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It's all in the Illustrated News, where the women are handsomer and the men more majestic, I daresay, than in reality.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No, no, that's nonsense. And I think that all persons of a certain station, like your wife's, should manifest their respect for the Heir Apparent to the Throne, and to his bride, by attending at least once.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I really don't see what we have to do with royalty, beyond paying the Queen's taxes.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Now, Henry, don't give way to such vulgar, radical, democratic notions. Loyalty is next door to gentility, and I have noticed that persons who scoff at such things generally become bankrupts sooner or later. I assure you I have observed it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I shall note your observation. How shall we put it? Persons who don't look after sovereigns will find themselves without banknotes.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I tell you, dear, don't turn everything into fun. I know that you have much more strength of mind than I have, but don't laugh at me when I say that I own I should like to hear the children read about Mamma at breakfast the next day. “Mrs. Henry Naggleton, by Lady Pugbury.” It is an event in a woman's life.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: A Lady's life, my dear.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.stage: (makes a ball of her handkerchief and throws it at him.)
sp.p: The real difficulty is, that I have no jewels.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Cornelia never said that.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No, but I'm not Cornelia, nor cornelian either, and there's a joke for you, Mr. Henry. Now, dear, of course we must hire them for that day, and I should like you to go with me to Spark and Facet's, and arrange all that—they pay more respect to a gentleman than to a lady.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: And expect the gentleman to reciprocate the extra payment. Now, I tell you seriously, Maria, the entire thing's absurd; but if it were not, I don't care about Lady Pug for a chaperone for you.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No, and if I were a girl, or a young matron without much position, I would not have her; but it is a mere form, and it matters very little who introduces the wife of Henry Naggleton. She stands on her own name, or rather his.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Chè sara sara, and if the Countess Russell should pay you any marked attention, or tell you that the Earl is dying to consult me on some treaty, say I quoted his motto.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: But what does it mean, Henry?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Does the translator of Carey's Dante— I mean of Dante—ask me that? It means that I suppose I can't help myself.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You are a good, dear creature. Won't the children be enchanted to see Mamma with a train and feathers?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, the whole business seems adapted for such appreciation—but are you going to move that Queen, or do you mean me to take her?

div.stage: [The day of glory has come, and we may say has gone, for it is seven o'clock, p.m., and Mr. Naggleton is quite ready for his dinner, and it is quite ready for him, and for his wife. He has shown no irritation at being kept waiting, however, but has been smiling, at intervals, with a very mischievous expression of face, as if he had heard something to somebody's disadvantage. There comes a tremendous ring, and in another minute Mrs. Naggleton in full Court costume, enters the Drawing-room.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Welcome home, Marchioness of Naggleton; you look splendid, but not exactly pleased. Your raiment is less ruffled than your brow; you have luckily escaped any crush, I conclude.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.stage: (taking off her feathers with anything but tender care.)
sp.p: I don't advise you to begin annoying me now.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Select your own date, my dear, but
what is the matter?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I tell you, don't aggravate me.

div.stage: Enter Carter.

sp.speaker: Carter.
sp.p: Please, m'm, the children want to know if they may come down and have another look at their mamma, before you change your dress.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No, they may not.

div.stage: [Exit Carter.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Rather hard, especially as you dwelt upon the pleasures of letting them see you in Court costume.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If you had behaved like an ordinary husband this would never have happened.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: If I knew what it was I would endeavour to defend myself.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I asked and begged and prayed you to go with us, and you wouldn't.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: The Lord Chamberlain ordered me and the masculine element in general not to come to the drawing-room.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: But he did not forbid you from seeing us down to the Palace as you would have done if you possessed the least manliness or good feeling.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: How the deuce was I to get into that pill-box of a carriage. There wasn't anything like room for Lady Pugbury and yourself. Your dresses filled it all up to the roof.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You could have gone on the box.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Six hours tête-à-tête with her coachman. Yes, I could, and I didn't.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No, and through your selfishness your wife's exposed to the humiliation of being the laughing-stock of all her friends.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Dear friends! But what have they to laugh at, I keep asking.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Why, good gracious, haven't I told you half a dozen times that we never got to the Palace at all, the crowd of carriages was so great?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You should have started earlier.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Of course say that. We were in the line by one, and it was your duty to have been with us, and make the police let us go on. Of course, I am a wife, and can't help myself, but Lady Pugbury is deeply offended, and I daresay will never speak to us again.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: We may survive that. But where was her own lawful and bandy-legged husband? If she wanted an extra servant on the box of her carriage, it was Pug's place.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: How should I know?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, dear, it's aggravating to have taken so much trouble for nothing, but it can't be helped, and you had better get rid of your splendour, and have some dinner.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I want no dinner.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Come, don't be childish. There will be plenty of Drawing-rooms, and another time we'll manage better.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I will never try again as long as I live.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You'll think better of it when you have dined—now you are weary and hungry, I daresay.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: All your fault, if I am.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Don't be unjust—don't say that.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I shall say what I choose, and I am not going to be put down by you.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Come, don't be rude, or I shall go and dine at the Club.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You can go and dine at Jericho if you like.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: The idea of a woman at your time of life flying out like a school-girl because she couldn't get into a room and make a curtesy.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You are talking like an idiot.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, I am repeating your words.
I think I had better write at once to the Prince, and explain that you and Lady Pug intended to be loyal, and beg that your absence may be overlooked. Carter can take the letter.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Loyal indeed. The Prince—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: My dear!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If it wasn't his fault, it was that of the haughty stuck-up nosed aristocratic peacocks about the Court, who are as poor as church mice for all their fine airs, and would be glad to borrow money of their betters, whom they insult.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Such awful sentiments make me shudder. Loyalty is next door to gentility, and we of the Blue Blood, we with a proud pedigree, niece of the celebrated man m---

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I have tried to make you a gentleman, Henry, but now I give up the task. Have your dinner, and go to the Club. I shall not come down again to-night.

div.stage: [Sweeps from the room, but the dignity of the exit is somewhat marred by her angry clutch at her unaccustomed train.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Ha! Ha! I oughtn't to be angry, this time. The event has avenged me. Piggy Farmer was right when he said he saw them, and that they hadn't a chance. Devilish handsome she looked though, and none the worse for the excitement of her wrath. The bandeau in her hair was effective; she is like adversity, also a toad, in respect to wearing a precious jewel in her head. I might have propounded that to her as a conundrum, but it will keep. I will go to the Club.

div.stage: [Does, a brute.

div.head: Part 14
XIV.—AT HOVE.
div.stage: Our friends have, like all other civilised people, been absent from the Metropolis for some time. They took a house at Eastbourne, for the season, but the defences which the doctors of that place made for its unhealthiness, convinced Mr. and Mrs. Naggleton that a locality requiring so much advocacy had better be left to the sanatory authorities. So they came on to Brighton. They have just come in to lunch.

sp.speaker: Mr. Naggleton.
sp.p: I don't seem to want any lunch.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It would be strange if you did, after eating all those apples and sweetmeats and rubbish.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I had only one apple, and one peardrop, which the children made me take.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Made you take! And you call yourself the head of a family, and pretend to guide and direct the rest. If you could not help indulging your old school-boy tastes, you might have some consideration for the children, and not stuff them with trash and spoil their dinners.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Why, you bought the apples yourself.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: But not to be eaten then. I meant them for dessert.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You didn't say so, and it was difficult to infer the fact from your immediately proceeding to distribute them among the kids.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Kids! Is that the language you wish your children to talk?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: They are none of 'em in the room.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It would be just the same if they were. I have noticed that. Mr. Snotchley quoted one night a line he had learned from some Latin classical poet which you would do well to study and act upon.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: What did the Latin classical poet say to Mr. Snotchley, my dear, I forget, I'm sure. Was it Varium et mutabile semper fœmina?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I daresay—it sounded like that, but it meant that the greatest reverence is due to young persons.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I am sure, my dear, I show the utmost reverence to young persons—and to persons who are not so young. There is no harm in kids unless they butt your legs.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Of course, you always take refuge in buffoonery.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, sometimes I take refuge in bathing machines, as to-day, when you dragged me out for a walk in spite of a sky that looked as black as you did at my making an objection.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: We don't come to the sea-side to stay in-doors all day, but to have the benefit of the fresh air. If you are so afraid of a little rain, you should take a Macintosh and an umbrella.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You lent the first to Mr. and the second to Mrs. Snotchley on Tuesday night, and neither have they had the grace to return.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Did you expect Mr. Snotchley to come out in a day like this?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, you made me come out in a day like this, in fact this very day.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: His habits are very different from yours. He has lived with the superior classes, who remain at home when the weather is unfavourable, or else go out in their carriages, while you have the mercantile habits of a man who is tied to business, and must go out to work like a clerk whether he likes it or not.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, I'm very depraved and demoralised, I know, but one's balance at the banker's is none the worse for one's neglecting the barometer.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am not reproaching you, Henry, I am only stating a fact, but you are so dreadfully thin-skinned that if I said the sun shone you would find something to complain of.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I should, if you said so, just now, my dear. I should complain of the absence of your usual veracity. The sun appears to me never to shine down here.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I know what that means. Another hint that you want to leave Brighton, and be back to your darling London.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I beg to say, Maria, that I do not hint my wishes, but signify them. When I deem it time to end our sojourn by the Coast, I will say so. In the meantime do not cry out before you are hurt.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Why, you have been as miserable as possible all the time we have been here.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Thanks to your efforts, I have not been particularly comfortable, but as I have made no complaint, I do not see that you need make any.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O, very well then, let us go back to-morrow.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: We cannot do that, having to pay for the house until Wednesday week. Besides
if you and the children are enjoying yourselves, that is happiness for me.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That's right, scoff at domestic feeling. I cannot think, for my part, what you married for.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, my dear, at this very long distance of time, I am really unable to tell you at a moment's notice—and I do not observe around me any particular aid to memory on the point. But I will endeavour to recollect, and inform you on some other occasion. Have you finished your lunch?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Because we might as well have the things taken away.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What for?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Because somebody might call.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Who?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: How should I know? Perhaps the polite and penitent Snotchley might put his aristocracy into his pocket and bring home my Macintosh.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: The fuss you make about that miserable Macintosh is perfectly unbearable. I will walk over and fetch it home myself, and take care how I lend any of your things again.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Don't walk, my dear, go in two cabs, for I'm sure one wouldn't hold you in your present state of temper.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I should like to know where you picked up that piece of vulgarity.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Why, my love? Do you wish to go and look for another piece like it?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I quite shiver when I hear you talking to the children, and I wait to hear what coarseness you are going to teach them next.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Bless me, how the sea air freshens up one's voice. I could take the chair at a Harmonic Meeting.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Yes, I do not dispute that.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I think there is one held somewhere near here. I've a good mind to go, and take old Snotchley with me.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: He go to such a place!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I'll bet you a pair of gloves he does, if I ask him.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You would not presume to ask him.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You shall see. I shall tell him that it is his duty, as an instructor of youth, to be acquainted with all the snares with which they might be tempted, and I'll undertake to bring him home by midnight slightly flavoured with Cavendish, which he will like as an aristocratic baccy.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Pray, pray, Henry, do not talk in that manner. You cannot imagine how offensive it is to my ears. Are you coming on the Parade?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: The swells will not be there yet, my dear.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You forget that we are not in Brighton, but have a long distance to walk, thanks to your taking a house in this ridiculous neighbourhood.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It was my fault, I suppose, that Eastbourne became dangerous. It was my fault, I suppose, that Brighton was so full that we couldn't get a house.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Had we gone to Scarborough, as I begged that we might do, we should have been in no danger, and we need not have hidden ourselves in a hole like Hove.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You are quite alliterative, Maria, and I scorn to remind you that you utterly refused to go to Scarborough, when I offered to go there.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Yes, after the scene you made, and the terrors you expressed about the frightful expense, and then at the last minute pretended to give way—of course no woman of ordinary spirit was going to be treated like a child.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: If I had treated you like a child, I should have taken you just where I pleased, instead of coming to a place which I detest.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Naturally you detest Brighton, because it is a place where the upper classes come, and where a certain decorum and refinement prevails, and you cannot lounge about the Parade at all hours in short trousers, with a distorted wide-awake hat, a dirty old shooting jacket with gaping pockets, and a clay pipe.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: That is a gross exaggeration, but that would be more sensible than rigging oneself out like a Bond Street lounger, and parading up and down for hours, smirking at acquaintances, staring at painted women, and listening to a band playing tunes that you'd send a policeman to stop if they were performed before your windows in town.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You have no refinement, Henry, and it is one of your misfortunes.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: As you say, one of them. And what do you say to the paint on the women's faces?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Are you going to accuse me of painting?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, my dear, no, no
Even the lily, we read, may be painted, but not, I think, the decidedly developed, not to say full-blown rose.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I make no answer to insults.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I never offer any. Can't you take a joke?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I delight in true wit, but not—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Not in wit whose essence is truth. But you won't come to the point. What do you, a respectable British matron, say to walking about among those animated paint-pots in pork-pie hats.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Will you inform me how much worse it is for a woman to lay vegetable rouge on her cheek, because it is pale, than for a man to apply walnut pommade to his hair, because it is grey?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I wish you would leave my dressing-table alone. I never can keep a single thing—somebody comes and takes it. I didn't know the hair stuff I bought was walnut pommade —I asked the man for anything that was good for the hair, and I thought walnuts were as harmless as anything else. What inconsequent nonsense you talk.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I? ahem!

div.stage: [And they go on the Parade, and the humbled Mr. Naggleton is quite civil and polite all the afternoon.

div.head: Part 15
XV.—ON POLITICS.
div.stage: The Scene is laid in Mr. Naggleton's “Library,” an imposing apartment measuring twelve feet by ten, and containing a book-case and a boot-rack. Enter to Mr. Naggleton, Mrs. Naggleton, bearing a newspaper.

sp.speaker: Mr. Naggleton
sp.stage: (who is at his desk, reading a large Blue Book and making enormous notes therefrom).
sp.p: Ah, Maria. One moment. “Witness considers that the outlay upon a Royal Palace ought to be under the control of the vestry of the parish in which such palace is situate.”
And I concur. Now, then, my dear, what is the next article?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You need not remind me of your tradesmanlike education; but—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, my dear, but if you use such language, I must take leave to remind you of the rules of syntax. An education cannot be like a tradesman. Devote the energies of your remarkable mind to the consideration of that proposition.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Be pleased to stop talking nonsense, and just tell me what this means.

div.stage: [Shows him a paragraph in her newspaper.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I am pleased to see that you can condescend to take an interest in any periodical besides Le Follet, my dear. What is this?

“We understand from good authority, that at the approaching general election, one of the candidates for the representation of the great and liberal borough of Finsbury will be found in the person of Mr. Henry Naggleton, the eminent drysalter of Lower Thames Street, and of Westbourne Gardens, Hyde Park. This gentleman's political principles entitle him to the confidence of the electors, and his oratorial powers are of no mean order. We hope that he will stand.” Well, I am sure that it is very pleasing to be introduced in this favourable way to the notice of the public.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Mr. Naggleton!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: He hears with ears.

div.stage: [Rather uncomfortable, however, in spite of his quotation.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You cannot mean to tell me that this— that you have given the slightest authority for printing such a disgraceful and disgusting paragraph.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Modestly waiving the newspaper's compliments, I see nothing to object to in the paragraph. All its statements are true. I am a drysalter, and those are my two addresses.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: The newspaper ought to be prosecuted. As if the vulgarity of printing your trade, and trade address, was not enough, you must drag my house into the business.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, your house came out of the business.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry, this is no common affair. I generally speak my mind, and there is an end of it, but this becomes serious, and you must be good enough to abstain from insulting me with jokes. What does this paragraph mean?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: What it says.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What! You have the face to sit there and tell me that you are going to squander the money which ought to be your children's, to buy yourself into Parliament for such a place as Finsbury. That it should come to this!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: That what should come to what?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O, well, that is enough. I must consult with my family as to what it is my duty to do. I feel crushed and bewildered.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Consult your family, Madam? What do you mean by that? I have merely to inform you that if your family takes the liberty of intruding its impertinence upon me, I shall make very short work with your family, Mrs. Naggleton.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I cannot answer your violence, Henry. That it should come to this!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (we fear with a strong expression which need not be set down.)
sp.p: If you would cease to repeat that idiotic cuckoo note, and talk sense, I might answer you. If you can't, perhaps you will let me read.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry! Henry!

div.stage: [Looks earnestly at him, and then takes to her pockethandkerchief.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Maria, do not be so absurd. In the first place there is no harm done at present, and in the second there is none intended.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O—o!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: There is nothing unreasonable in a man's having an ambition to sit in Parliament, I suppose?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O—o!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Don't go on in that way, or you will compel me to act without consulting you. I had looked for your advice and assistance.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Mine! I help to ruin you and rob my children. Henry!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Ruin and robbery be—left out of the argument. I tell you that nothing is settled, but that if I stand for Finsbury it will be on the distinct understanding that I do not pay one shilling. Do you hear that?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It is well to treat me like a child, Henry, but I listen to the conversation that goes on around me. I understand your Jesuitry.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: And I don't understand the word.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Mr. Snotchley mentioned the other evening how these things are done. You do not pay. Of course not. But somebody puts a large sum of money into a bank, for bribing votes, and though you have no idea who has done it, you are bound in honour to see that he gets it again.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Mr. Snotchley has derived his experience from observing and probably participating in the corrupt practices of his patrons, the unscrupulous aristocracy, who—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry—it is a small matter at such a moment as this, but your whole language has changed, and you talk as if you were making speeches to the rabble.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Rabble, Maria, is not a term to be used in describing any portion of your fellow-creatures, and you will specially eliminate it from your vocabulary during my connection with political life.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Oh! That means that you are going to be connected with the lowest of the low. If you must move out of your own sphere into one for which you are ridiculously unfit, you might have tried for something respectable.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: For some pocket borough, I suppose, on sale by some friend of Mr. Snotchley's.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: There you might at least have been elected like a gentleman.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Certainly. I might have broken the laws myself, and caused a few hundreds of other persons to take bribes and to perjure themselves.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If you are so much better and more virtuous than other Members of Parliament, I wonder you condescend to join them.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: There are men, Maria, who will enter Parliament unstained by a single offence against the law, and if I enter it, I shall be one of that band.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Band, indeed, yes, a brass band, to profess such hypocritical virtue. Don't I know that you can no more get elected for Finsbury without the good-will of the public-houses than you can fly in the air?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Who told you that nonsense?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Is it nonsense? I am not to be fooled. Henry, I think it my duty to tell you that you must be insane to go on in this manner. I can account for your conduct in no other way.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: And who asks you to account for my conduct.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Everybody will ask me.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Who's everybody. Your family, perhaps?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Well, if they should show enough interest in my welfare and my children's to remark that you ought to be very rich to engage in elections—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You may ask them to show a little more interest, and promote your welfare and your children's by paying me certain debts which you know of.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And you would consign my relatives to incarceration that you may squander the money in the beer-houses of Islington.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: That speech is perhaps the greatest feat in the way of a flying leap that will be performed during the whole hunting season. Ha! ha! ha! What an old goose you are!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Pray, Henry, pray take advice.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: My dear, I'm quite well.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Think of the children. Why should their prospects be blighted for the sake of your foolish vanity. Don't fly out; you know I speak the truth, and only for your good. You are about as fit to be a Member of Parliament as I am to make a steam-engine. You have no seriousness; you can amuse people of your own sort with after-dinner speeches of not very refined humour, but you cannot speak so as to command respect, and as for politics, you know nothing but what you learn from newspapers. You will only be a laughing-stock, and it will be very hard upon me to hear you made a butt in good society.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Your unwifelike disrespect for me, and your utter ignorance on political questions I can pardon, with some pity, but please to leave the children's names out, or I shall leave the house.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Is it good grammar to say unwifelike disrespect. Can disrespect be like a wife?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Perhaps you will allow me to finish my reading?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Before you turn me out of the room, will you be so kind as to say what I am to answer when anybody asks me about the truth of the paragraph?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Ask them in return how they think I made my money.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What a question!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Never mind; ask it, and if they can't tell, say that it was by minding my own business.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And this is the treatment which a wife receives when she humbly creeps into her husband's room and ventures to ask for his affectionate confidence in a matter of such importance to them both. Well, well!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Affectionate confidence! Pelts him with abuse for an hour, and then talks of affectionate confidence.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And cannot a man of the world, and a husband, make a little allowance for the excitement of a wife whose mind has been suddenly troubled, as much for his sake as her own, and who beside is far from well?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I did not know you were not well, my dear Maria. You look the picture of health. Why don't you sit down?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You did not ask me.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Ask you! How can you be so foolish.

div.stage: [Gives her a chair.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Never mind now, dear, I must go up to the nursery. Don't be angry with me.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You do try me, occasionally, Maria, and really it is not the thing to try and drive me. If you had not flown at me as you did, I should have told you that before you came into the room, I had sent off a letter to the paper to contradict the paragraph. I have no intention of standing for Finsbury.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Well, I did not think that upon reflection you would be such an idiot as to offer yourself.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You did not?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No. But I am sorry you sent away the letter without letting somebody else look over it to see that you had expressed yourself with tact.
Mr. Snotchley will call in the afternoon, and he could have corrected it for you. However, I am glad that you have shuffled out of it somehow.

div.stage: [Exit, and shuts door.

[And on the whole it is as well that she did shut it. The enraged politician takes the oaths and his seat, but not in a way that would at all please that eminent theologian and bishop-stirrer, the Speaker.

div.head: Part 16
XVI.—UPON ROME.
div.stage: The happy couple are at Breakfast in their house in the fashionable locality in which we had last the pleasure of meeting them. Mr. Naggleton is, of course, reading his “Times.” Mrs. Naggleton has received some letters by the morning post, and has been meditating on their contents.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Naggleton.
sp.p: Henry, this is the First of August.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Maria, your chronology is indisputable. Moreover, I wish you many happy returns of the day.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Good feeling would dictate your avoiding a joke on that subject, Henry.
