sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: O, isn't it your birthday, my dear? But that is no reason why I should not wish you a happy return of the day, or of any day.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Happiness is a word for persons who are differently circumstanced from myself, Henry, but I am making no complaint. I merely reminded you that this is the first of August.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I had already learned that fact from the newspaper.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You may learn something else from it, I dare say, and be told that everybody but ourselves is out of town.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: If there is such a personal statement, my dear, I shall come to it presently, and I will then consider whether I ought to call the editor to account.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I think, Henry, that by this time you have known me quite long enough—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: My dear, I am incapable of admitting anything so rude.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Quite long enough to be aware that nonsense may delay what I may wish to say, but cannot prevent it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Have I ever refused my tribute to your pertinacity, my dear Maria? What do you wish to say now?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What it would not have been necessary for me to say, if I had had a different husband.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, you have an indifferent one. Agreed. Go on.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Indifferent, indeed, Henry. Indifferent to the state of my health, and that of his children.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Agreed, again. How hard he tried to get you from Mrs. Owleybird's party on Friday, when morning was dawning. And how pleasantly he handed Dr. Peter Grievous a cheque for thirty-seven pounds on Saturday for medical attendance. Your husband is all that is objectionable, but make the best of him while he lasts.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It is, I am sure, as much for your own sake as mine that I wish, if we are to visit the Continent, that we should not delay until the season becomes unhealthy.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: But suppose we are not to visit the Continent. Who's the Continent, that we owe him so much attention?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O, go to Southend, if you like, or stay at home, and shut the front shutters. I don't care.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Very well, my dear. As that is the case, I will consider those two excellent suggestions. At first blush I seem to prefer the shutters.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Is this the way in which we ought to converse, Henry? I am sure that I hear nothing like it between other couples. Mr. Winkletop can be playful in answering his wife, but it is affectionate fun.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Playful darlings!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And though Mr. and Mrs. Gough-Hawe are always laughing, they understand one another, and she has no wish ungratified. But you are always in an attitude of fighting and resistance.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Ajax defying the lightning; eh? Am I so ferocious? Well, look on me as another classical sculpture, the Dying Gladiator; and now, what can I do for you before I die?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Ah! Those allusions remind me of what would indeed make me happy. But it is of no use talking.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Never mind that. Talk. What is it? Do you want to go to M. Brucciani's new gallery, and see his casts?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Shall I ever see Rome? Here is a letter from Mrs. Bosser, who is there, and who writes in perfect raptures of its treasures of art and of antiquity.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Mrs. Bosser? No, no, Maria. Come.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: There is her letter.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, thank you. Lord Palmerston says he has had no time for twenty years to read anything but manuscript. I prefer print, not being eighty. But Mrs. Bosser. I think it was that eminent lover of art who told us Landseer's dogs were clever, but not equal to those of Animal Carracci, and I am sure it was that eminent antiquarian who told us that Hereford Cathedral was being restored in the Renaissance style.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Your spiteful memory supplies an argument against you. We go abroad to learn.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Some of us, like yourself, my dear Maria, have nothing to learn, except how to stay at home.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am too painfully conscious of my own deficiencies to accept an insincere compliment dictated by a mean economy.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Then I would avoid exposing those deficiencies to fellow-travellers, as you would do in a place like Rome.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: There was a time, Henry, when you pretended to take pleasure in showing new objects to your wife, and making her enjoy them by your clever explanations, and the information that you have so curiously acquired.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: There is nothing curious in it. I have endeavoured to read books, and I have tried to remember what was in them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Men's minds are so much better trained than ours, and you learn to apply your knowledge at a moment's notice. I know nothing more delightful to a wife than to be able to turn to her husband for anything she wants to know, and I am sure that if you and I could see Rome together, it would be something to remember all our lives.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: My dear, I am a humble but faithful adherent to the Church of England as by Law Established. What could I say to myself, if your Protestant principles should be sapped by the Scarlet Lady, and you should seek refuge in a convent?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I took the veil once, my love, and my courage has not been so very well rewarded that I am inclined to try again; so do not be afraid, or perhaps I should say, have no hopes.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, but look here now. Another year I would not object. But we are too late for Rome this year.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: We can never be too late for the Eternal City. Mrs. Bosser is enchanted with it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: The Eternal City and Widow Bosser. “Powers eternal, such names mingled.” Really, Maria, the idea of a woman of your intellectual power being led by that idiot, at whom you used to be always laughing.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am not led by her, Henry.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, you are; and I cannot understand the ascendency she has acquired over you. Even Snotchley, the milk-and-honey boy, has remarked that you dress at her, repeat her foolish sayings, and surrender your own judgment to hers.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If you permit another person to make disparaging remarks to you about your own wife, I say no more.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: But I did not permit it. The words were hardly out of his mouth when I gave him my mind on his impertinence, and he will not repeat it; but to do him justice, he apologised by urging that he only noticed what everybody else said, wondering at your humility.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That settles the question.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: And you will not give further cause for such tattle by following Mrs. Bosser to Rome at her bidding.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I will go to Rome to show how utterly I despise tattlers and backbiters.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I do not quite see it in that light.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If you have the spirit of a man you will. And I will write to Mr. Snotchley this very morning, and tell him among other things, that while Mrs. Snotchley owes me for the very shawl in which she came to my party—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: What shawl, my dear?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What shawl? Have men no eyes? Did you not put it on her great shoulders yourself, and quote something ridiculous about not displaying her beauties to the moon?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I understood you to say it was your shawl, my dear. The one I gave you on your—birthday?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I never liked it, as you know.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You told me it was sweet.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I didn't—or I hadn't tried it on—or one changes one's mind. At least she said she liked it, and I let her have it at the price you said it cost, and she owes me the money.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Not a bad bargain for us, if she pays that, and takes a year's credit. Maria, I don't like this.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Don't like what?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I say nothing about ladies selling things —I suppose you have your own code of high manners. But I made you a present on your birthday, and you pretend to be delighted with it, and then you sell it. I shall remember that.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No doubt you will. It will be an admirable excuse for stinginess for the rest of your life.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I have never been stingy, and you have no right to say so.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I shall say what I like.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Still, at your time of life, you should set your children an example of speaking the truth.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: So I do.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I deny it. And I repeat that you did not do a wife-like act in parting with a present of mine.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: A wonderful present, certainly, to make a fuss about. And I am not a child, or a slave, to have a thing given me on condition I always watch over it, and never lose it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: If your temper had been given you on those conditions, my dear, I fear you would be without one. I am glad to find that you are not.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Will you buy a Continental “Bradshaw” to-day, and ascertain about the route to Italy?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I will not. No, Maria. Every walk we might take in Rome would remind me of this painful disclosure. As you have said, the Eternal City would be an eternal memory. The Tarpeian Rock would recall domestic treachery. The Via Sacra would show me Mrs. Snotchley going to church in my shawl. Bitter thoughts would have a long Triumph in the Forum; and the inevitable ball at the banker's would make me think of the cheque Snotchley owes. Southend, or the Shutters, or even Paris; but no Rome.
sp.stage: [Exit under cover of his own fire; and then, outside, and with a disreputable grin—
sp.p: But to quote a Roman poet, Sic me servavit Apollo.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I did not think I should get him even to Paris; but there's nothing like asking for more than you want. That is safe, and I love Paris. I wonder whether Mr. Snotchley did say a word of all that. I will call and lunch there, and perhaps she will pay me. Lucky I did not tell him that I had sold the shawl to her at half-price.

div.head: Part 17
XVII.—ON VOLUNTEERING.
div.stage: Mr. Naggleton has dined in Town. Mrs. Naggleton has dined with the children. He has returned about Six o'clock. Scene—The Drawing-Room.

sp.speaker: Mr. Naggleton
sp.p: Anybody called?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Who should call at this time of year, when every decent person is out of town?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I asked an answer, not a question.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No one has called on me.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What do you want?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I want the bell answered. That is one reason why I rang it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: The servants are busy.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Now, how should you know? Surely such domestic details are beneath your notice. I doubt whether you know how many servants we have. Here is one, however.
Has anyone called for me?

sp.speaker: Housemaid.
sp.p: Only the taxes, Sir, and Mr. Wyndham Wareham. He said he hadn't a card, but his love, and you was to be punctual at eight to be grilled.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I understand.

sp.speaker: Housemaid.
sp.p: And there's a large parcel of clothes for you, Sir. I have put it in the dressing-room.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: What a blessing this rain has been. The country must look lovely.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That concerns those who are allowed to see it, not me.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: All in good time, my dear. The taxes. I thought I had paid them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O dear, don't apologise for leaving your wife exposed to duns. A man's home is the last thing he thinks of.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: The first and the last, if he's a good man.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: But the insolence of officials must be borne—a woman cannot help herself when a husband is unwilling or unable to meet his debts, —but I will not bear vulgar people coming and leaving joking messages with my domestics.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, I told you it was not the thing when we were walking out last night, and you left word with Mrs. Snotchley's Martha to say that you supposed her Mistress had been washed away by the rain.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Will you be good enough to tell Mr. Wareham that if he chooses to persist in calling here, he had better behave like a gentleman?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I shall tell him nothing of the kind.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Then I shall.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I can't prevent you making an unlady-like speech to anybody, but that is scarcely the way to impress him with a sense of his error.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: We shall see. I am not afraid of him, though you are.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Am I? I didn't know it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Other people do.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Bless them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I wanted to call on the Baltimores this evening, but as you have Mr. Wareham's orders to be somewhere else, of course that is out of the question.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Not for that reason, but because I do not choose to call on any but decent people.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And what have you got to say against the Baltimores, pray, except—I admit that that is bad enough—except that they are your wife's friends.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You just said that all decent people were out of town.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: The Baltimores go on Thursday, and that's why I want to see them, but it is so like you to shelter yourself behind a mean catch.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Your image is rather confused, my dear, and savoureth less of your favourite, Dante, than of your favourite, Dundreary. Sheltering behind a catch would be difficult, even to an expert cricketer.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Trash!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (struggling to be civil, but not exactly succeeding.)
sp.p: True. But King Solomon has told us to answer a—wise person according to his wisdom.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I don't believe there is another man in London calling himself a gentleman who would allow people to leave ridiculous messages at his door to make a servant grin when she delivers them.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I have already given you my opinion on that kind of message, so we need not re-open the subject. If you like, I will leave you at Baltimore's, and call for you in an hour and a half.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I shall do no such thing.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I said what I would do, my dear, if you liked.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Certainly, that you may go to some low haunt or other with Mr. Wareham, and come back to the Baltimore's in a state of vulgar excitement.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Serene in good intent, Maria, I defy that taunt. We are going to see a nobleman, a real nobleman, my dear, and to listen to his aristocratic and improving conversation for the time I have mentioned.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: As if any nobleman would receive Mr. Wareham and you!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I am going by the divine creature's express invitation, not to say command, Mrs. Naggleton. Now!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I will believe that when I see it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Duly thanking you for your wifely confidence and respect, I will at once permit you to see it. There!

div.stage: [He gives her a note, in which he is informed by the Adjutant of the Westbourne Volunteers that they are to come to drill that evening at Eight, when the Colonel, Lord Silvertongue, will be present.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.stage: (having read it with that contemptuous haste so delightful in woman.)
sp.p: I did not think that you were such a Fool. You must excuse the word. I know no better one.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, that is an excuse, I admit. And I deserve the word, for—for several reasons, one being before my face. However, there are limits to everything.
I will send up your cheque from wherever I may be to-morrow. Good evening.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Now, Henry, is not that cowardly, and just like a man? A wife does not exactly see the rationality of something he is doing, and instead of defending it, he runs away, at a time of year, too, when she is without a soul to speak to.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: She had better speak to her own soul, at least to her conscience, and ask what she deserves.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I was wrong. There! But I have been far from well all day, and you startled me so with the sudden paper, that I did not know what I said. How can you be so cross?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Cross is not the word.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Haven't I begged your pardon? But why could you not tell me that you were going to be a volunteer?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I had planned what I foolishly thought had been a pleasant little surprise for you and the children when I came down in the uniform. But I ought to have known how little I could calculate upon your abominable temper.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And if my temper is not quite what it was, what has spoiled it but the trials of my married life. And you ought, therefore, to be the last person to revile me for it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You say what is absolutely untrue, and no woman ever had less to complain of.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Ah! you little know what people say—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: And I care as little.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.stage: (has a capital rejoinder; and if she were only in Paris, but as it is, only says),
sp.p: My dear Henry, do not set the strength of your mind against mine. Allow me a woman's privilege of being unreasonable. And come, if I let you go to Lord Silvertongue's, will you promise not to be later than ten.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: If I am, tell the servant to go round for you.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Now that's unkind, after what I have said—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: After what you have said? I don't think so.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Yes it is. Go and have your drill—I suppose that is what Mr. Wareham meant by grill —and make friends with Lord Silvertongue, and ask him to come and see us.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Not very likely that he will.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I don't know why. It is a fine noble family; but he is only the second peer, and his grandfather made his fortune by honourable commerce, just as you have done. Where is the wonderful difference between you?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You wicked radical, you; I wonder that fat Peerage there, which you study so hard, doesn't explode and blow you away.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I respect the aristocracy, dear, but to depreciate the great middle class would ill become the wife of a mercantile man—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Or the niece of a celebrated acc---

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Acclimatiser of infant aristocrats.

sp.speaker: Mrs.N.
sp.p: Do you know that I think poor Uncle would have liked to be called that? He was fond of sonorous expressions.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: The taste is hereditary.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Don't begin scolding me again. You might invite me to come and see you—grilled. O! I must tell that to the children.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, yes, certainly, but you had better wait until the Corps is a little more perfect in certain exercises.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Such as the goose-step, dear? I think I have heard of that manœuvre.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: That is—they call it the balance-step without gaining ground—that is an early accomplishment.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Show me how you do it; do, dear.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Never mind now. I will another time. Now do you wish me to go with you to the Baltimores?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Of course I do. They are going to Brussels, which is only a little Paris after all, I believe, and I want you to say to them, carelessly, in your humourous way, that a little Paris is not big enough for us, and that we are going to the great one.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: But we are not.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O yes, dear, we are. You know you promised that, and you never go back from your word to me. You promised me faithfully.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Bad English.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Then we'll mend it with good French. Was not that clever, Mr. Henry? And mind you bring out what I tell you neatly to the Baltimores. I shall lead up to it, so look out. By the way, what was the large parcel Sarah spoke of?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: My uniform.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O, go and put it on—you must, and you shall. I should like to see it of all things. Couldn't you go to Paris in it?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Certainly not.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I don't know why. The French are a military nation, and would take it as a compliment.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I have no desire to compliment the French nation.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: But you have a desire to compliment me. Go up and put the uniform on, and knock at the children's door and tell them to come down. Then we'll go to Mrs. Baltimore's. Would you mind having a cab, as I am rather tired?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: As you like. Be ready at half-past seven.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: All right. You are quite like the Duke of Wellington already in your prompt orders.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I wish I wasn't like him in having to invade France.

div.stage: [Exit.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Yes, I should think I would have a cab. Fancy walking in daylight with a man who has on a uniform for the first time! But I have clenched Paris. Men are very weak. If he had called me a fool, I would have made it Rome before I spoke to him again. But we must put up with them. Come in, darlings.

div.head: Part 18
XVIII.—ON SPIRITUALISM.

sp.speaker: Mr. Naggleton
sp.p: Do you see anything remarkable about me, Maria?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You look very slovenly, and you have come up-stairs with muddy boots, but there is nothing remarkable in either.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: In either of my boots?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: In either proof of your disregard of the decencies of life. I witness it too often.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Ah, don't scold now, but listen to something interesting.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I prefer to go to bed. It is very late.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, it was not much later last night when you informed me that you were ready to go out.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O, if you wish to quarrel, I submit. I have no spirits to resist.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Resist, nonsense. Spirits is the word, however. I have been with the spirits.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What nonsense are you talking?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: None. I tell you I have been at a Manifestation, and I have seen some very extraordinary things.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You cannot mean that you have been at a séance.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Why can't I?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: But you don't?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: But I do.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Then you have been to one of those meetings, where they sit in the dark, and supernatural things are pretended to be done.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Are done.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry, I did hope that I should never have to despise my husband.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, I rather hoped so too, at least not this husband.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I trust that you are joking with me.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You don't encourage me in that practice, my dear. I am telling you a simple truth. I have been to a spirit-manifestation, and I thought that though you are not usually much interested in anything I say, you might like to hear about this.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I have heard enough.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: O, very well, just as you please. I am sorry now that I did not go over and have a cigar with Browner and Poldoodie, instead of making the best of my way home.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Mr. Browner I know enough of to wish to know no more. The other person with the ridiculous name I never heard of, but you have a talent for picking up low acquaintance. That is a trifle however.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It is not a trifle that you should tell a spiteful untruth. And Poldoodie is not a low acquaintance, at least you did not think so when he took you down to dinner at the Pankeys'.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What a falsehood. That was Mr. Hoister.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: All the same. In our facetious way we call him Poldoodie, which is some kind of Scotch for oyster.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I thought him too much of a gentleman to allow vulgar liberties to be taken with his name.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Then you thought wrong, you see, as you often do. A true gentleman is not a starched stiff-back Snotchleyfied prig, but a man who can distinguish between good fellowship and impertinence.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If he associates with your set, he has plenty of opportunities of appreciating the latter.
I suppose you will go to bed when you are ready.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I suppose I shall. Good night, if you are going.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Put out the gas, unless you are afraid.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: What should I be afraid of?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Your conscience.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: What's my conscience got to do with gas? What has the Gas Company's own conscience to do with it either, if you come to that, for it's very bad and precious dear?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I see that you wish not to be left alone, and I do not wonder.
If you play these tricks with your nerves, you will soon be a pitiable creature.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I am that, but not on account of nerves. My nerves were never better in my life. What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Try to carry it off so, but I know you better. You have been dreadfully frightened, and it serves you quite right.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Frightened at what, in the name of all that is ridiculous?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: How should I know what wicked folly you have been witnessing? I only see that it has had its effect on you, being a weak man, and that you are all in a flurry. You had better go to bed. I will light you to your door, and you can keep the gas burning all night—that extravagance is better than your being terrified into illness. Will you take anything sedative?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, some brandy-and-water, and a cigar, which I'll have in the study. Don't be nonsensical. I am about as much frightened as you are. Will you hear what I have seen?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I had rather not, but if talking relieves you, go on.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I knew she wanted to hear all about it. Well, Poldoodie called—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Oblige me by keeping that vulgarity for your friends, and by giving persons their right names.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Hoister, then, but I think the other name is more aristocratic—hoister reminds one of a crane at a warehouse.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: As I do not frequent warehouses, I am not reminded of anything of the kind.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: He called and asked me to go to the séance, which was at a private house in Pall Mall, so I had a chop with him at the Reform Club.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: In those boots? But I believe that the radical and republican fashion of that place tramples upon all external decencies—the floor is sanded, I suppose.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: How can you talk such idiotcy? I wish you could see the Reform kitchen.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You don't mean that you condescended to dine in a kitchen?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, I don't, though I have dined in worse places. We had one bottle of champagne, and one of claret, between three, Browner being the other, and some liqueur.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Your wife had one glass of pale ale.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: More goose my wife, who has the cellar-key.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Which she will never use again after the insult and abuse which followed her last use of it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: There was neither, Maria. I only said that you might have given a pack of schoolboys something cheaper than my best port. But confound your memory for old grievances—you never remember pleasant things.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I have so few to remember.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You are as lucky a woman as I know. Well, we went over at eight, and found about twenty people assembled. The Medium was brought in, and the operator made a little speech, and then the lights were put out, and we sat in a circle, with our hands joined.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Fancy a pack of men being such fools.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: There were some women, too, for I held hands with two.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Nice sort of persons to come to such a place.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You'd go to-morrow, if I would take you.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I hope, Henry, that even if you commanded me to go, I should know my duty too well to obey.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I won't try you, my dear, especially as I disapprove of women sanctioning such things. After a time we heard some scratchings and knockings, and then music began to play in different parts of the room, the instruments moving about.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Confederates, of course.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I don't know whether they were Federals or Confederates. Then some luminous hands appeared, and waved about.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Old gloves stuffed with bran and rubbed with phosphorus, and stuck on the end of wires, or lazytongs.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I cannot say. Then a strong and mysterious wind passed by, and they said it was the spirits' wings.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Pair of bellows, most likely, blown by some of the party.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: And then there was a very faint light, and some said that they saw a human figure moving through the air.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Your own child could do that trick better, in the daylight, with the kite he blows out into the shape of a boy. Upon my word, I can hardly listen with patience to such trash.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: And then something hit me on the head.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am very glad of it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: And then some said that hands were touching them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No doubt they were. Pickpockets. The business seems invented for genteel pickpockets.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: And at last a hand came to me and touched mine.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If you had had any spirit you would have caught it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I did, and held it tight.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And of course let go, just as you do everything.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Not exactly, for there it is.

div.stage: [Flings the Spirit-hand on the table. Mrs. Naggleton snatches it up.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: As I said. No, where are my scissors.
No, wool, not bran, and springs, and you see where it was broken off from whatever was holding it. Why, you can smell the phosphorus quite plainly.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, but don't rub it on my nose.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: But didn't anybody know that you had caught the hand? Of course you couldn't keep the secret to yourself.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I held my tongue. The business came to a sudden end, and we were told that the spirits were unhappy, and that a compact of honour had been broken. But as nobody confessed, there was an end.

div.stage: (only on his cheek, though)

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Strong language, my dear.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I mean it to be strong.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Mean the same about my grog, my dear.

div.stage: [Exeunt, to celebrate the Truce.

div.head: Part 19
XIX.—AT THE ZOOLOGICAL.
div.stage: Scene—The Zoological Gardens. A beautiful afternoon. Sunday. The clock over the Camel says half-past three. A large gathering of the Upper Ten Thousand. Mr. and Mrs. Naggleton, the Misses Emmeline and Cecilia Naggleton, and the Masters Edgar, Walter and Peter Naggleton, all in spring array, enter, and advance up the Broad Walk.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Naggleton.
sp.p: Pierre, do not hop. This is Sunday.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, remember, Peter, nothing hops on Sundays, except the birds, who know no better, having no private tutors.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That is right; make him laugh at his mother's advice.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: On the contrary, my dear, I would imprint it on his memory. Though I don't know why he shouldn't hop, like the little hills.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am not acquainted with the family you mention, and I do not wish them proposed as models for my children.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Nicely you attend to your Brady and Tate, Mrs. Naggleton.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Pray, Henry, abstain from such profanity while your children are within hearing.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Profanity is in intention, my dear. Mr. Snotchley had the sense to quote that, when you were good enough to laugh at his old joke about Paul being a cricketer, because he stood up for the Eleven and was bowled, and Rhoda stood at the wicket.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That was real wit, and I wonder you understood it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Oh, wonderful husband, that can so astonish his wife! Shakspeare.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I think you might do better than mouth out Shakspeare on Sunday. Emmeline, come away from the bears!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Bless me, they came here to see the beasts, and they shall see them. Jump, Syllabubs.
Here, Walter, take this fourpenny bit, and see how many stale buns that young lady will give you.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Teaching your children to break the Sabbath in that manner!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I am teaching them to break nothing except buns. Isn't a bear to be fed on Sunday, especially when he has fallen into a pit? That's a man, Walter—a bun a-piece. Where's the stick? Here we are. Now, Mr. Bear, climb for your lunch!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I shall walk on to the chairs on the grass. I can at least avoid witnessing what I disapprove.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: All right, dear; go and stare at the bonnets, while we finish our secular duties.

div.stage: [Exit Mrs. N.

sp.speaker: Walter.
sp.p: Come on, Papa, don't give all the buns to these stupid beasts. I want to give something to the ippopotamus.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: So you ought, in return for the h you've taken away from him.

div.stage: [Shout of laughter from the children. Mrs. N. looks angrily up from the plateau below, and Mr. N. thinks it wisest to rejoin her.

sp.speaker: Emmeline.
sp.p: O, Mamma, what do you think Papa said?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Nothing, my love, which I wish you to repeat. Walk on quietly, two and two.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Too-too-too dears, like a penny trumpet.

div.stage: [Another shout.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: This behaviour is more disgraceful, Henry, than I could have believed your conduct ever would be. Really, this is not a place for you. You must suppose that you are in some low tea-garden, among the rabble.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, my dear. These are the Gardens of the Royal Zoological Society, Regent's Park, N. W., and I am a fellow, and it's your fault if I am not a jolly fellow. It's the most enjoyable place in London, or, as you would say, in this extensive metropolis, and I came here to enjoy myself, and—deducting conjugalities—so I do. Go where you like, children, but mind, don't put your fingers between the bars of a single den—and I say
, mind this. If one of you children gets eaten, I'll never speak to that child again.

div.stage: [Loud shout and away go the young ones.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Catch me coming here again with you.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I didn't ask you to come.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No, I am not accusing you of any such civility.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You asked yourself to come, and I wish that at the same time you'd asked yourself whether you couldn't come in a decent temper.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You are the only person, I have often said, who ever dared to find fault with my temper.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Perhaps, as I have often answered, because I am the only person on whom you ever dared to try it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That speaks well for your dignity, as the Head of the Family.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It speaks better, perhaps, for my patience, which some day you will try too far.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It is so manly to threaten a helpless woman who is chained for life.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: If she is, she needn't rattle her chains incessantly. But come, it is Sunday, and you have been to church, and earned a right to neglect all the minor duties, such as kindness and politeness. Won't you take a chair?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Not in front, certainly, that all your set, Dick, Tom, and Harry, may come up and claim acquaintance with one.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You were glad enough to know my set once.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You thought so.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You said so. Excuse me for believing it, and two or three other things.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Ah!
sp.stage: (A Cyclopædia of Useful Knowledge in that little noise).

div.stage: [They take chairs behind the rail, and observe the elegant company seated, passing, and re-passing.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: If it wasn't Sunday, I should say “My eye, what a pretty girl!”

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Painted flirt!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Lovely hair, come.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Bought—I hope paid for.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: She is very like Lady Annabel Lee whom you rave about.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I never rave about anybody, and that person is as like Lady Annabel as I am like your grandmother.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Hm!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I wonder who that distinguished-looking man is? You never know anybody, so it's no use asking you.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I know in this case.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Pardon me if I don't believe it. He is evidently somebody. His dress and manner are those of the best society.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: How should you know?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I may be unfortunately circumstanced as regards my own position, but I have a lady's instinct, which never leads me astray in forming a judgment.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, it is right enough this time.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Of course, it is. Whom do you suppose that gentleman to be?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I don't suppose about it.
sp.stage: (Calls out to the Distinguished Somebody, “How are you, Blobby?”)

div.stage: [The Distinguished Somebody looks round, and Mrs. Naggleton turns red with shame and anger. But the Distinguished Somebody comes up to the rail, and shakes hands with Mr. Naggleton.

sp.speaker: D. S.
sp.p: Hawful ot, ain't it, my boy?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Stunning! I have the superior honour of introducing you to my wife. Mr. Blobbings, Mrs. Naggleton.
sp.stage: (She shudders a fraction of a bow.)
sp.p: And how's tallow?

sp.speaker: D. S.
sp.p: Sputtery, sputtery. But sink the shop on Sunday, my bricksy-wicksy! Be genteel, my boy, if the house is a-fire. Splendid day, M'm.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Very fine. Where are those children?

div.stage: [Walks off, and is shortly afterwards overtaken by the faithful Mr. Naggleton.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Sorry you went off, my dear. Blobbings wanted us to come over to Camden Town, and dine at half-past four.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I detest practical jokes as a rule, but that gentleman showed all the self-possession and ready wit of a man of society, and I can forgive him.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Blobbings a gentleman! Why, he's in the tallow line!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You need not meanly adopt his clever ruse, and try to carry it on. I hate imitation.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It is not one of your usual faults that your meaning is difficult of comprehension, my dear. But upon the present occasion I must remark Davus sum, non Œdipus.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I wish you would not quote Latin without asking Mr. Snotchley whether you pronounce it right. I am sure that is wrong; my ear tells me so.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Confound Snotchley and your ear? What about Blobbings?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That gentleman was a stranger to you, but instead of resenting your low trick, he humoured it, and pretended to know you. His affectation of vulgar talk showed me that, because it was overdone—not even one of your friends in the City could be quite so hideously coarse. It was clever, but the aristocracy are never taken aback.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, but I am. By Jove! Not Blobbings? I'll fetch him. No, I can't, for he has hurried out to be in time for dinner.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Lucky! Say no more about it, but be thankful that your vulgarity escaped castigation—some gentlemen might not have let you escape so easily. If he had pulled your nose for calling out to him, you could not have complained.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I should not, certainly.
sp.stage: (Passes an “abstract resolution” in spite of Mr. Gladstone.)
sp.p: Yes, you are a clever woman. Ha! ha! ha! ha!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Don't make such a noise, Henry, dear. People will think that one of the wild beasts has got loose.
sp.stage: (They walk to a more removed ground.)

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Which day did you ask the Snotchleys, the Baltimores, and the Silverdales for?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Hang it, can't I know when I'm to give a dinner?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Don't be so violent—next Thursday, a quarter to eight.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: All right.
sp.stage: (Makes a note of it on a letter.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Now may a wife be allowed to ask why the question is put?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Perhaps I may have a pleasant surprise for you, in the presence of an aristocratic friend.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.stage: (feels that the Federal armies have close round, but resolves on one dash.)
sp.p: You will ask no person to my table without consulting me and obtaining my sanction, and if you do so I will insult him.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I put the party off by to-morrow's early post if you do not to-night send an invitation to Blobbings.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry, you are very unkind.
sp.stage: (Uses handkerchief, but slightly, as she is in good society.)
sp.p: Can you not accept a harmless little joke, meant to pay you out for the way you showed me that I had mistaken your friend for a gentleman—I mean I am sure he is very well as a man of business—but you know what I mean.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I do, Maria, and also what I mean.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And you will put off the party?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Except on the condition I have made.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: But I accept the condition. I am not ashamed of your friends, though in your ill-nature you accuse me of being. I shall be happy to invite Mr. Bobbin.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Blobbings? You will?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Certainly, or any other friend you wish. Do I give dinners for my own pleasure, or to support your credit? You know I dislike them, and prefer a chop at one with the children. Of course we will ask Mr. Bobbings.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Blobbings.
Well, we shall see about it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I will send the note to a pillar-box to-night, and he will have it at nine in the morning. I shall see his address in the Directory; you need not think about it again.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, I don't know that he is just the man to meet the Silverdales and Baltimores.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: He shall come.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No; on second thoughts, he shall not.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: He shall come. After what you have said, I will put the party off if you do not invite him.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I will invite him, then.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I understand, and when he will get the note. I'll ask him myself.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I tell you it won't do; he's a vulgar beast, and I wouldn't have him for a hundred pounds.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: He comes, nevertheless. A wife is not to be played with like a child or a toy.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Maria! I will be obeyed, or—

div.stage: Enter (dignus vindice nodus) Emmeline and Cecilia running.

sp.speaker: Both Children.
sp.p: O, Mamma! O, Papa! Come, come! run, run!

sp.speaker: Both Parients.
sp.p: What, what! Where, where?

sp.speaker: Both Children.
sp.p: Peter, Peter!

sp.speaker: Both Parients.
sp.p: What, what?—speak!

sp.speaker: Cecilia.
sp.p: The Blue-nosed Monkey has torn off his—

sp.speaker: Both Parients.
sp.p: Nose?

sp.speaker: Emmeline.
sp.p: Hat, and he and his wife are eating it.

div.stage: [General amnesty, and both armies rush off to attack the Bluenoses.

div.head: Part 20
XX.—ON THE AFRICAINE.
div.stage: Scene—The Breakfast Table.

sp.speaker: Mr. Naggleton
sp.p: I see that the Africaine went well on Saturday night.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I suppose that after thirty or forty performances the singers ought to know the music.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I dare say they will. Only as the season will be over this week, I don't see how they are to have all that practice.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What are you talking about? It is more than two months since the opera was produced.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: In Paris, yes.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.stage: (looking up with a terrible glance, and repeating, slowly.)
sp.p: In Paris—yes. Be good enough to give me the paper for a moment.
sp.stage: (She takes it from his unresisting hand, and reads a few lines.)
sp.p: I see. I did not understand you. I could not for the moment believe it. I see. I might have expected it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Expected what? That the opera would come out? Well, you might; Mr. Gye is in the habit of keeping his promises.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Yes, Mr. Gye is.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: What a tone! Is that meant as a crusher for the other house?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You understand me, I have no doubt. Let us drop the subject.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: The Irishman protested against being picked up before he had fallen down. I protest against dropping a subject before it has been picked up. I don't know what you are driving at.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Your evasion is too contemptible. But you are the master of the house, and have a right to deny your family any amusement. We can only submit in silence.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I must quote the Irishman again, and say that pigs may fly, but they are very unlikely birds to do it. Submission in silence is one of your favourite habits, isn't it?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Do you wish it? I have read somewhere that the slave's silence is the tyrant's danger.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You great idiot, don't talk such trash. I am a frightful tyrant
, I know, and you are a trampled slave. If you can't be rational, hold your tongue, and let me read the newspaper.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It's a man's privilege to escape in a fit of violence, as I have read that some fish get away by making a cloud of mud.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I compliment you on your zoology. The Gardens have set you studying. But now that the storm is over, will you be good enough to tell me what it was all about?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If I could ever respect hypocrisy, it would be from its association with such perseverance. I am making no complaint, Henry.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You always say that after giving me five-and-twenty minutes' jobation. Well, you have no complaint, but only a grievance. What is it?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Nor have I a grievance. But I think, as a mother—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Now for something pleasant. “Mother's” always the cue for malice.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: As a mother, I may be allowed to say that you should keep your word with the children, and not teach them to look upon your most sacred promises as idle words.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Said so.
Putting this and that together, Maria, I gather that you accuse me of having made some promise about the new opera.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And of having broken it. That is all. But as I said, you are the master of the house, you have the purse, and our enjoyments are dependent on your will and pleasure. We have no right to murmur at your caprices.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You are a sweet creature, and you have the gift of saying sweet things. But I begin to recall something of the sort.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am glad of that.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Why should you be glad? If anybody has been disappointed I am sorry, but the whole business went out of my head. You should have reminded me.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O, thank you, no. I have had too much experience of the sort of reception any little hint of that kind meets. I am not always in a state to be scowled and stormed at.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Tell me what I promised, and when.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It is really of no consequence, Henry. What signifies the addition of one dull evening to so many?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: May I ask you to answer me?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It does seem so strange that you should have forgotten, but if you say that you have, of course I cannot disprove it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I promised—what?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You do not remember that wonderfully clever and sparkling thing in Punch—the plot of the Africaine, with the most extraordinary illustrations by that gifted artist Mr. Du Maurier? How odd! The children were enchanted with it, learned it by heart, and played it before Mr. Snotchley and the Baltimores. It was a perfect success.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I was not present.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Well then, perfect with that drawback. But I mentioned it to you, and you immediately said that they should see the real opera when it should come out. I admit that I was rather surprised at such a liberal promise, but once made, should it not have been kept?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It went out of my head, I tell you, and you ought to have reminded me.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Certainly you should all have gone. At least I would have tried to get a box, though on a first night of a new work by Meyerbeer, boxes were no doubt at a premium. But the truth is that I forgot all about it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Quite natural that you should.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I understand you, Maria. Perhaps, however, you may some day discover that on that very Saturday I remembered my children to a better end than taking them to a theatre. But I have long since ceased to make confidences where they are received without sympathy and gratitude.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am very sorry, dear Henry, that you should think us ungrateful. I am sure that we are much obliged to you for food and raiment, and all that you are so good as to give us.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I believe that I am too severe in wishing the punishment of flogging inflicted on husbands of the lower class who are nagged into striking their wives. I myself, with all the advantages of education, habit, and self-command, find it difficult to abstain from using a very strong expression. However, that is over.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I will take care to remember what I have escaped, Henry, and avoid such risks. I would not have mentioned the opera, if I had thought that reminding you of a promise to the little ones would have put you into such a rage. But
, if you are hot, your coffee is cold. Send your cup across. I see that the season is nearly over. I will keep the papers from the children, and they will perhaps forget all about it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: They shall do nothing of the kind, for the Africaine is played again to-morrow, and I will get a box.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: A single stall would be cheaper, dear, and you will hear as well, and see better.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: A stall?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: For yourself. We are all going to Mr. Snotchley's, who has promised, after tea, to read Rasselas to us, and he reads so beautifully (not theatrically, as you do), that I want the children to have the treat.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Snotchley and Rasselas; and they are to be kept from real enjoyment for that! I shall take them myself.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Not, I trust, against their own consent as well as their mother's.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Do you want to make me believe that they would sooner go and sit in a stuck-up room, hearing an old frump drone over the dullest book in the world, than go to the theatre and see a fine show?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If my superintendence of their education has been efficient, they would prefer foregoing an amusement to committing a rudeness. But I will ask them presently, and I will tell you their answer.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, don't. I am aware of what it will be. Don't teach them hypocrisy. It's early days for that. What night are they not liable to be bored by Snotchley? The opera is played on Thursday, and again on Saturday, which is the last night of the season.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You refused to let me accept Mrs. Baltimore's invitation for Thursday, because you said you were engaged at a business dinner.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I forget what I said in my desperation, when I was driven into a corner to avoid a man who gives South African wine.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That seems fastidious in a man who likes Hungarian and Greek wines.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Just a woman's nonsensical talk. Because I don't like one novelty I mustn't like another. I wish I may never drink worse liquid than my Hymet, or my Erlauer. Snotchley himself praised them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: He is a gentleman, and would not dispraise your wine at your own table.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: But he would behind my back, you mean. I believe that.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry, a gentleman puts the best construction on language, until he is quite certain that a worse was intended. I mean that Mr. Snotchley could not help speaking well of what you were giving him, and, I must say, were yourself praising, which was not in the best taste.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I beg your pardon. I shouldn't praise my own house, or my own furniture, or my own wife, or my own children.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You never did the last two things. I acquit you there.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: If I don't talk, I'm a beggar to think, like the Welshman's owl. But as I was going to say, wine is a sacred thing, and not subject to conventionalities. If a man gives me bad, I'll tell him it's bad, and vice versâ, and if he is offended, he is not a man whom I desire to know in this world or any other. And I will speak about my own wine as frankly.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: As you scarcely ever give a party, it does not much matter.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: We've had six or seven since Easter. And you always ask the same people, who sit in the same places, and tell the same stories. And after hearing Snotchley relate for the seventh time how his grandfather picked up George the Third's walking-stick on Windsor Terrace, the fierce excitement of that narrative somewhat abates.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I like old friends, and I do not expect you to like the tone of good society.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Your good society's tone is rather a monotone—which reminds me that we were talking of an opera. I will get the box for Thursday.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Believing you truthful in saying that you were engaged, I arranged to take the children to the St. Winkle and St. Welk Schools, to hear a lecture by a missionary from the South Sea Islands.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Have they been so very naughty?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Who, the islanders?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, the children.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Two severe punishments in one week, Rasselas, and a missionary! I am sorry they are growing up so demoralised.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I can joke on any subject but the moral characters of my children. I do not mind being sneered at for my attempts to improve them.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Rasselas was dull enough, but the author was honest and the English is highly superior, but a fat missionary with a pack of cant about savages whom he perhaps never saw, or perhaps sold rum to, is really not a party to come between the children and the opera.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: They heard you say you were engaged.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Then I shall say that my engagement is off.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Two falsehoods—the first to your friend, the second to your children.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I like that from you, who told Mrs. Silverdale that we were going out of town on Monday.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That is just what I expected. A wife struggles to save her husband's credit, and her excuses are dashed in her face.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: My credit! What next?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Every person will have left town next week, except those who are detained by pecuniary difficulties. I dare not ask whether this is your case, because any reference to such things draws on me a storm of insult, but I did not desire that the Silverdales should suspect it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha! ha! ha! You should have lived in the days of the Chevalier D'Eon, my dear. I am sure you would have beaten him when he was a fencing-mistress.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: There is what my late uncle used to call a metallic ring in that laugh, Henry, which does not speak badly for the children's future.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: That is neither here nor there. But that phrase was rather neat in the late lamented acc---

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Henry!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Accelerator of existence. By the way, did you notice that the excellent Locock is not elected for the Isle of Wight? That eminent accoucheur yields to a believer in the Immaculate Conception.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If you can introduce an insult to my family, I am sure of hearing it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Where's the insult? I can't say I respect your uncle's memory, because it was so bad that he forgot to leave you anything—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Club jokes are very flat by daylight.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, daylight has its advantages for old jokes and old—
—old clothes. Talking whereof, we'll go and hear the grand old Jew on Thursday.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I have already mentioned our engagement.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Then, for the last time, what do you say to Saturday?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I object to going out on Saturday nights. It is usually impossible to reach this door before twelve o'clock, and then it is Sunday.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Riding in a carriage is not wrong on Sunday, is it? You did not say so when we were going to the Star and Garter yesterday.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: The Star and Garter is not a theatre, so your sophistical argument entirely falls to the ground.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Then we'll leave it there, and now that the subject has been discussed, we'll drop it. You will make the children understand that you and not I have prevented their seeing the Africaine, and that Rasselas, Fat Missionry, and Cant stop the way. I will tell you on Wednesday what I think of the Opera.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You don't mean to say that you would go by yourself?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You advised it just now, and your advice is good. I mean to take it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No, take a box for Thursday, you cross old thing.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: And the Fat Missionary?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Well, if you think there is any doubt about his having been to the South Seas, we might be encouraging humbug.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: And that should never be encouraged, Madam.

div.stage: [Winks, and exit, and they all heard L'Africaine, and rave about Lucca.

div.head: Part 21
XXI.—ON RETURN FROM THE COUNTRY.
div.stage: Mr. and Mrs. Naggleton have been spending a few days at the House of a Friend in a Southern County. They have returned to-day, and converse after a late dinner.

sp.speaker: Mr. Naggleton
sp.p: I drink your health, Mrs. Naggleton, and congratulate you upon your safe return to your household gods.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Don't talk nonsense, and above all, heathenish nonsense.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, we will say your household goods. There's no harm in that, especially as furniture is one of your idols.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I have no idols, and I do not see why a woman is to be sneered at for wishing her house —her husband's house—to be properly furnished. You certainly lose no time in throwing off the mask which you have been wearing for three days.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I only wish I had worn one, for I am scorched worse than the sole we have been trying to eat.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It was not the cook's fault. She had not known that we were coming, and then she was ordered to get a dinner in a hurry.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: And why did she not know?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Because she was not written to.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: And why was she not written to?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Because you, with your usual ridiculous indecision, could not say which day you would leave Mr. Appledram's.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I like that. I do like that. When you yourself were watching and dodging to find out whether the Appledrams were going to give a dinner-party while we stayed. You only agreed to go when you found that it was a hopeless date —next week, or you would have stopped till now.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Of course I misconducted myself. I always do. Of course I scorched the sole.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Never mind about misconduct. The sole, yes, because when you had actually succeeded in making up your mind, you would not let me telegraph.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Telegraph to a cook!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Why not? Ha! ha! She has a battery de quizeen of her own. Ha! ha!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: We are at home, Henry, and there is no further excuse for the childish nonsense which you have been drivelling for three days.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, we must all laugh sometimes. I thought that we had been tolerably jolly.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: To be laughed with is one thing, but it is another for a wife to sit and hear her husband laughed at.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: He deserved to be laughed at for taking such a wet blanket into the country with him. No I retract. I did not mean that—I take it back. But you are a refrigerator, you know, or what it is now the fashion to call a thermantidote.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Don't resume the mask; be as insulting as you please.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: What nonsense you talk about masks. What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Hypocrisy, Henry, has been described as the tribute which Vice pays to Virtue. But the tribute is too often paid in bad money.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: My wig! but that's an epigram of the first water. I saw that you were reading a good deal in the country.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I can smile at such a taunt, Henry. I don't affect smartness. It would not do for both of us to be pretenders to wit.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Very good, I'm sure, very good and very affectionate and wife-like.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: How you fly out at the slightest attempt at retort upon your eternal attacks. But I am told that such is the way with joke-makers of a certain order; they are the most thin-skinned creatures going.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I am not flying out, though I was never much more inclined to go out.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Pray do not let me detain you. I hope I can make allowance for what you must have undergone in being obliged to be civil to your wife from Saturday to Wednesday.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I should always be civil to you, and a good deal more, if you would let me, but your temper is so extraordinary that you construe a kind speech into a wrong, and turn it off with a pleasant mixture of sarcasm and ice—not delightful even in weather like this.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Remember that you are drinking your own wine, which is fiery, and not like Mr. Appledram's.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Do you mean that I am excited?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I simply mean to give you a caution, as you are speaking fast, and with needless violence.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Appledram's wine is very good, but it is neither better nor even dearer than mine. Shall I fill your glass?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: No, I thank you. If your taste does not detect the difference, mine does; and after taking his for some days, I would rather keep to water for a time.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, no, Maria, second Mrs. Naggleton, M'm—you shall not stir me up again on the wine question. You are a first-rate authority, of course; your esteemed aunt, from whose house I had the honour of marrying you, keeping such a splendid cellar at the bottom of her wardrobe.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: The remark is manly. And you are perfectly well aware that my aunt has ample means, and that it was upon conscientious motives that she would not lay away money in a cellar.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I respect her motives, but cuss her Marsala.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You are not asked to drink it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, I have that luck, certainly.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Though a father might have been unselfish enough to put up with the harmless whim of an old lady who could do much for his children, and he might have paid her an occasional visit.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I have heard and read a good many odd things, but I know no nation that makes it incumbent on a father to poison himself for the sake of his offspring. But I have frequently told you that you could visit the old creature whenever you pleased.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I trust that I need no permission to visit my relations?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: But you don't go.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That is my business.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: What's the good of talking stuff? You know, as well as I do, that her idiotic will is made.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Wills may be done away, I believe.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Good gracious, partner of my bosom and expenses! Do you suggest to me a terrible crime? Are you a Lady Macbeth? Would you have me go down to your devotional but disagreeable old aunt, make her Marsala worse than it is by an infusion of laudanum worse than her conversation, discover her will in a disused nightcap, and destroy aunt, will, and cap at one fell swoop? No, it is tempting, but tempt me not.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: If you have finished that ranting, which is not in the least like Mr. Buckstone—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It is an excellent imitation, now.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You think so, and are told so, I dare say, at the Club, when you have provided drink for the members, but you really have no power of imitation.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It is a great story, for I imitate one person to perfection.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Who may that be?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Job.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I request that you will not be wicked.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: My dear, it was not Job who was that, but another member of the household, according to Shakespeare.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Shakespeare had better have avoided such topics, and many others; but you will fly out again if I venture to say that he was anything short of perfection. Mr. Snotchley says that is an article of faith with people who get sentimental in taverns.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Mr. Snotchley is an ass and a prig. Snotchley on Shakespeare is a treat. Don't quote his folly to me.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I said so.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Said what?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That you would grow violent, if a word was said against your superstition. Never mind, I will be more considerate of your feelings than you are of mine, and not make fun of your idols.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: The woman who speaks lightly of Shakespeare is—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Your wife, and not in the habit of being shouted at, nor will she bear it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I wasn't shouting.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You don't know what you are doing, I think. Do put the stopper into that bottle.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: We have had three pleasant days, Maria, and I think you need not have finished the out with a row.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: The Out with a Row. I don't know whether it is true that we always return to our first loves—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I wish some of us did!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Gentlemanly! But I am sure that we return to our first language. You must fancy yourself in the time of my predecessor in the dignity of your wife.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No, my imagination is not so strong as that, in the presence of evidence to the contrary.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Yes, surely, you must, and that you have just returned by a twopenny boat from Greenwich, after an elegant repast on tea and periwinkles. Don't weep at the sweet recollection. The Out with a Row.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: My first wife had her faults, I dare say—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I really have no desire to enter into the biography of that person.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: But you shall hear, Madam, once for all. She was considerate, affectionate, and playful—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Playful darling.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: And as unlike you in manner and talk as possible.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I trust so. I hope so. I am delighted to hear it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: She was a very good wife, Madam, mind that. You are—

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am—what, Sir?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: The wife of a very good husband, Madam, who will be d---d if he will stand this sort of thing. I do not know what time I shall be home to-night, but I have the key, and if anybody is up when I return, I will discharge every servant before ten to-morrow.

div.stage: [Leaves the house.

div.head: Part 22
XXII.—ON GREENWICH.
div.stage: The Scene is the Coffe-Room at the Ship, Greenwich. The London Season is over, nevertheless nearly all the tables are occupied. The Distinguished Couple have the little table near the large one in the bow window.

sp.speaker: Mr. Naggleton.
sp.p: Is the flounder zoodje to your taste?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: O, of course, I like everything. I come to such places far too seldom to presume to be critical.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: That is the true secret of enjoyment.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I hate secrets.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You keep one very well.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What may that be?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Il segreto per esser infelice.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: What a torture it is to hear you try to speak Italian, Henry.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I beg pardon, I'm sure. I forgot that I was talking to the translator of Cary's Dante —of Dante, I mean. Now, some of the salmon zoodje? I assure you it's very good.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Good enough for me, I suppose, but not for you, as you turn up your nose at it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I'm not very hungry, and I am reserving myself for the whitebait.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I should wonder if you were hungry.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: True, for I made an excellent breakfast.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I don't mean that, and you know it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I am sure you mean something pleasant —in return take some lobster cutlet. Your health, my dear.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Pray do not take wine without eating. You are not in your own house now, and you ought to be careful.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: No fear, the wine here is very good— your health, again, in the driest of Sherry. Don't send away that fish pudding, it looks insipid, but it's very delicate.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I shall take nothing else, unless you behave like any other husband. What do you mean by sticking me in my chair like a child, and telling me to take this, that, and the other, while you only look on amused?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Well, we came out for amusement, didn't us? However, here is something that suits this child,—the salmon cutlet and pickles. What a noble thing is pickles! Even as a retort, the word has great classic power.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: How strange it is that if there is one vulgar thing in a whole dinner, you are sure to pounce upon it. I think I have heard Mr. Snotchley liken that kind of mind to a leech, which instinctively fastens on the unhealthy part.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: If old Snotchley had introduced such a delightful illustration at dinner time, I should have suggested his walking into the garden; but as the speech is yours, I will only drink your health once more, and advise you to take some eel—the sauce is curious. I'll have some of this Spey boy, with the Tartar—an article to which I am accustomed.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That is vulgarity, if you like. A piece of rudeness may sometimes be redeemed by its novelty, but there is nothing so intolerable as worn-out impertinence, particularly when one cannot escape.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You don't want to escape, I hope, my dear. An Admiral's great grandchild talk of deserting a Ship!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That, now, is one of the best things I ever heard you say, Henry. You see that I can be just.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You shall hear me say something much better this moment, Louis!
sp.stage: (That prompt and intelligent foreigner is instantly at hand, smiling and listening.)
sp.p: Some of that Champagne.
sp.stage: (Louis is already deep in those cool halls where Psilas shuns the day.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Champagne already!

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: It can never come too early, or too late —never mind genteel conventions, which are kept up by screws to save their liquor.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Liquor. Can't you say wine?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Easily, but it seldom is wine in screws' houses. Silverdale, for instance, always makes a charade of action of my conundrum, “How to make gooseberry fool—Hand your friend what you call Champagne.”

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I don't know—Captain Silverdale moves in good society—

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: So does a footman.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: And I should think, therefore, that he would make no mistake.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I don't say that he does—nobody wants to be helped twice, and he earns the right to his return dinner, cheap.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Your ideas are fearfully coarse, Henry.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Coarse things wear well, my dear, and my ideas about Silverdale and some other folks have lasted me a good many years. Now, Louis Valet, fill those glasses up to the top, and let us see the beaded bubbles winking at the brim. Your health again, Mrs. Naggleton. Is not that good lining for human nature?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I am not partial to Champagne, especially at the wrong time. This is much better than our own, of course, but not better than we taste at other houses.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: That's all you know about it—it's out and out.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: The thing for an “Out,” then.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.stage: (The fact is that he was a little ashamed of a certain scene, and this dinner is a kind of peace-offering.)
sp.p: Let by-gones be by-gones, as the last horse said to the jockey at the Derby.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: The Derby! I wonder you recal that, then.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You will survive me, Maria, of course, but if I had to write your epitaph, I don't think I could be respectful to your memory. Some more whitebait?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Why do you give me disagreeable things to remember?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: This is one, I suppose?

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Do you expect me to be grateful for being brought to Greenwich when everyone else is out of town?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Is it my fault that we remain in town? Are you going to throw your aunt at my head? I have told you that there's nothing serious the matter with that respectable Miss Flaggerty, but you insist on remaining.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: I know my duty to a relative whom I respect.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I have no objection, but do your duty without grumbling. And, as for the season, I am sure that there are several women in the room at this moment who are dressed better than yourself.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: That is a happy thought to console a woman with.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Ha! ha! More Champagne? Yes, it would have been a clumsy speech, certainly, only you can say with the vain Irish girl in the story, that this is not the dress you've got at home.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: These persons are mostly provincials.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: You talk of them as if they were criminals —as Cornelius O'Dowd describes Cook's excursionists, who, he tells foreigners, are taken to be gradually dropped all over the Continent.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: They are quite unlike the class one would have met here a month ago.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Yes, they look healthy and happy, and are thoroughly enjoying themselves, poor unhappy creatures. Let us hope that some day they may know better things, sit down without appetite, eat without pleasure, drink without laughing, and go away worse bored than when they came.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Those are your radical prejudices against the manners of the upper classes.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Let me give you some devilled bait. The fish are not what they were, but as the hymn says, Satan finds some whitebait still for Quartermaine to do. Hush! it is not wrong to joke about it. Dr. Watts was a Dissenter.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: You may sneer at my attachment to the Church of England.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I never did anything of the kind.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: But you cannot shake it.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Shake the church, my dear? I should be very sorry. But I wish the cook had given another shake of the pepper-pot.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Your palate is vitiated, and requires unnatural stimulants. These fish are very hot.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: Louis! Pweever!

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: It was lucky that you gesticulated as well as spoke, as he would never have known what you meant. Why not have spoken English?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I preferred French.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Then why not have spoken French?

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: So I did.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: Your pronunciation is something awful.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I am glad that there is something awful about me, a ray of the Olympian Jove, as it were. How jolly good this Champagne is. I could drink it in oceans.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
sp.p: How foolish you are! I can see, now, how it is that you are led away by Wyndham Wareham and the Club lot, until you take much more than you ought, and come home as you did last night.

sp.speaker: Mr. N.
sp.p: I was home before you, any how.

sp.speaker: Mrs. N.
